text: The highest permanent town in the world is probably La Rinconada, in the Andes mountains of Peru. It sits at about 5,100 m, higher than Mont Blanc, the tallest mountain in the Alps, and right beside a [[glacier|glacier]]. Tens of thousands of people live there, many of them working in small gold mines.

If you mean a big city, the answer is El Alto in Bolivia, at about 4,150 m. Nearly 900,000 people lived there at the 2024 [[census|census]], on a flat plain above the city of La Paz. Both places show how far people will go to live and work, even where the air is thin and nights freeze.

st.prompt: People born and raised in the Tibetan highlands cope with thin air differently from visitors. How?

options.t: They breathe faster and widen their blood vessels instead of making extra red blood cells
They have a third lung
They hold their breath to save oxygen

st.reveal: Visitors to high places make extra red blood cells, which thickens the blood. Many Tibetans don't. Their bodies breathe more and push more blood through wider vessels, thanks to genes their ancestors passed down over thousands of years.

myth: The highest capital in the world is Lhasa or Kathmandu.

Kathmandu is only about 1,400 m high, and Lhasa is not a national capital. La Paz in Bolivia, at about 3,650 m, is the highest seat of government. Bolivia's official capital, Sucre, sits lower, at about 2,800 m.

sec.t:
La Rinconada has no proper roads in or out for parts of the year, no full sewer system and no central heating. Temperatures drop below freezing most nights. People come because of [[@gold-where|gold]]: miners dig into the mountain hoping for a lucky find.

Many workers there are paid under a system called cachorreo. They work for weeks without regular pay, then get to keep whatever ore they can carry out on one day. The town grew fast in the 2000s when gold prices rose, which is one reason nobody is quite sure how many people live there.

Water boils at only about 83 °C up there, instead of 100 °C, because the air presses down less. That means rice and dal take much longer to cook, and a pressure cooker is a real treasure in a high kitchen.

People whose families have lived high up for thousands of years have adapted in different ways. Many Andean people have large chests and more red blood cells. Many Tibetans and [[@people-sherpas|Sherpas]] don't make extra red cells. Instead they breathe faster and move more blood through wider vessels.

Scientists found that many Tibetans carry a [[gene|gene]] variant, in a gene called EPAS1, that helps with this. Oddly enough, it seems to have come from the Denisovans, ancient relatives of humans who mixed with our ancestors tens of thousands of years ago.

India has high towns too. Leh, the main town of [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], sits at about 3,500 m. Flights there arrive in the morning, and visitors are told to rest for a day or two before doing anything tiring. Villages in Ladakh and Spiti, like Komic and Korzok, sit at well over 4,000 m.

Across the border, Lhasa in Tibet lies at about 3,650 m, the same height as La Paz. In the USA, the highest incorporated town is Alma in Colorado, at about 3,160 m (about 10,400 feet). And the highest people who live anywhere still sit thousands of metres below the summits of the [[@mountains-tallest|tallest mountains]], where no one can live for long.

text: Some [[atom|atoms]] are unstable. Over time they change into a different kind of atom.
Nobody can say when one single atom will change. But in a big crowd, almost exactly half change in a fixed time, called a [[halflife|half-life]].
Count the old atoms and the new ones, and you can work out how much time has passed.

quiz.prompt: You start with 1,000 atoms of a clock atom. After two half-lives, about how many are left unchanged?

options.t: About 250
None at all
About 500

quiz.reveal: After one half-life, about 500 are left. After the second, half of those remain, so about 250. Each half-life halves what is left, so the atoms never quite run out all at once.

d.try: Put 50 coins in a box, close it and shake. Tip them out and remove every coin that lands heads up. Count what's left and write it down. Repeat until no coins remain. Each shake is one "half-life". Draw a graph of your results and see the curve that scientists use to read atom clocks.
myth: Radioactive things glow green.

Most radioactive materials don't glow at all. The idea comes partly from cartoons and partly from old clock dials, which were painted with radium mixed with another substance that glows when radiation hits it.

sec.t:
Think of a huge crowd of coins. Toss them all, and remove every one that lands heads. You can't say which coin will go next, but you can be sure about half will go each round. Toss after toss, the pile halves again and again: 1,000, then 500, 250, 125.

Unstable atoms behave in a similar way. Each one has a fixed chance of changing in any period of time. With billions of atoms, those chances add up to a smooth, predictable curve. That's the clock.

Carbon-14 works for things that were once alive, up to about 50,000 years old, like wood, bone or cloth. Potassium, uranium and other atoms date rocks millions or billions of years old.

Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, nearly the age of Earth itself. So in rocks as old as our planet, about half the original uranium has turned into lead. Measuring tiny crystals of [[@rocks-oldest|zircon]], which trap uranium when they form, has revealed the ages of the oldest pieces of Earth and [[@earth-age|the age of Earth]] itself.

In 1896, the French scientist Henri Becquerel noticed that uranium salts left marks on photographic plates kept in a dark drawer. Something invisible was coming out of them. [[@marie-curie|Marie Curie]] studied this further, discovered new [[element|elements]] such as radium and polonium, and named the effect radioactivity. In 1903, Becquerel and Marie and Pierre Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.

In the early 1900s, the physicist Ernest Rutherford realised that this steady change could measure time. In 1907, the American chemist Bertram Boltwood measured uranium and lead in rocks to estimate their ages. The first rocks had been dated, and they turned out to be far older than most people had believed.

Heat, pressure and weather barely change the decay rate. That's why it's such a trusted clock, used to date the [[@iridium-evidence|asteroid layer]] and [[@cave-art|ancient art]].

Scientists also cross-check. If two different atom clocks in the same rock, such as uranium and potassium, give the same age, they can be confident it's right. Different labs, different methods and different countries keep arriving at the same answers.

text: Soil is made from rock that has been broken down over a very long time, mixed with the remains of dead plants and animals, plus water and air. Living things do much of the work: roots, [[fungus|fungi]], [[bacteria|bacteria]], worms and insects all help turn bare rock into soft, crumbly earth.
It is slow. In many places, nature takes hundreds of years to make a centimetre of soil, and sometimes up to 1,000. That thin layer feeds nearly every plant and animal on land, including us.

st.reveal: The UN's Food and Agriculture Organization says soil can take up to 1,000 years to form a single centimetre. Rock breaks down very slowly, and living things need time to mix in. That is why soil lost to wind and water is so hard to replace.

d.try: Shake up some soil. Put two spoonfuls of garden soil in a clear jar, fill it most of the way with water, close the lid tightly and shake. Leave it overnight. By morning you'll see layers, with tiny stones at the bottom, then sand, then fine silt and clay, and bits of plants floating on top.
myth: Soil is just dirt, a dead mix of crushed rock.

Healthy soil is full of life, including bacteria, fungi, worms and insects. They break down dead material, hold the soil together and feed plants. Without them, crushed rock would never become good soil.

sec.t:
Every soil starts with rock. Heat by day and cold by night make rock expand and shrink, and tiny cracks form. Water seeps in. In cold places it freezes, swells and splits the rock further. Rain is slightly acidic, so it slowly [[dissolve|dissolves]] some [[@minerals-everyday|minerals]] too. This breaking down is called [[weathering|weathering]].

Plants join in. Lichens, tough partnerships of a fungus and a tiny plant-like partner, cling to bare rock and release [[acid|acids]]. Roots push into cracks and widen them, like a wedge. Over centuries, solid rock crumbles into stones, then [[@sand-where|sand]], silt and clay.

Charles Darwin spent decades watching [[@earthworms|earthworms]]. His last book, published in 1881, was about them. He showed that worms drag leaves underground and swallow soil, passing it out as fine, rich castings. Over years, they bury stones and slowly mix the soil from top to bottom.

Their tunnels let in air and rain, and give roots room to grow. Ants, termites and beetles do similar work, especially in dry places where worms are fewer.

Dig a deep hole and you'll see that soil has layers, which scientists call horizons. On top lies a dark layer of fallen leaves and humus. Below is topsoil, where most roots and life are found. Under that is subsoil, paler and harder, and then broken rock. At the bottom is solid bedrock.

Topsoil is often only a few tens of centimetres deep. A few centimetres of it can hold more life than all the metres below.

Different rocks and [[climate|climates]] make different soils. In the Deccan, ancient [[@deccan|lava]] has weathered into black [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]] soil. It is sticky when wet, cracks when dry and holds water well, which suits cotton. Along [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]] and other big rivers, [[@floods-why|floods]] have spread fine, [[@soil-types-india|fertile alluvial soil]] over the plains for thousands of years.

In Kerala, heavy rain has washed many minerals out of the ground, leaving red laterite soil. Blocks of laterite can be cut and dried into building bricks, and many old houses there are built from it.

In the 1930s, [[@usa-dust-bowl|farmers on the Great Plains]] of the United States ploughed up [[@grasslands|grassland]] and planted wheat. When a long [[@droughts|drought]] struck, the bare soil dried out. Strong winds lifted it into huge black dust storms, and the region became known as the Dust Bowl.

Soil that took centuries to form blew away in a few years. The US government set up a Soil Conservation Service in 1935 to teach farmers to protect the ground, with [[@what-if-no-trees|trees as windbreaks]], crop rotation and ploughing along slopes. People who first [[@farming-began|began farming]] thousands of years ago depended on soil, and farmers still do today.

d.try: एका तिरप्या ट्रेवर शर्यत लाव. ट्रेच्या वरच्या टोकाला एका रांगेत एकेक चमचा पाणी, मध आणि टोमॅटो सॉस ठेव. मग ट्रेचं एक टोक उचल आणि कोण सर्वांत वेगाने वाहतं ते बघ. पातळ पाणी म्हणजे हवाईचा लाव्हा. हळूहळू सरकणारा चिकट मध म्हणजे स्फोटक उद्रेक घडवणारा दाट मॅग्मा.

बहुतेक लाव्हा इतका हळू सरकतो की लोक चालत दूर जाऊ शकतात. खरा धोका असतो तो गरम वायू आणि राखेच्या वेगवान, होरपळून टाकणाऱ्या लोंढ्यांचा. त्यांना पायरोक्लास्टिक प्रवाह म्हणतात. शिवाय वरून पडणारी राख आणि नदीच्या खोऱ्यांतून धावणारे चिखलाचे लोंढेही तितकेच धोकादायक असतात.

sec.t:
सोड्याच्या बंद बाटलीत वायू विरघळलेला असतो. दाबामुळे तो आत टिकून राहतो. बाटली उघडली की बुडबुडे फसफसत बाहेर येतात. जमिनीखाली खोलवरचा मॅग्मा अगदी असाच पाण्याची वाफ आणि इतर वायू धरून ठेवतो. तो वर येऊ लागतो आणि दाब कमी होतो, तसे त्या वायूचे बुडबुडे बनतात.

पुढे काय होईल ते मॅग्मा किती चिकट आहे यावर ठरतं. हवाईसारख्या ठिकाणचा पातळ मॅग्मा बुडबुड्यांना सहज निसटू देतो. तो [[lava|लाव्ह्याच्या]] लालभडक, चमकत्या नद्यांच्या रूपात बाहेर ओघळतो. दाट, चिकट मॅग्मा बुडबुडे कोंडून ठेवतो. दाब वाढतच जातो, आणि शेवटी मॅग्माच्या ठिकऱ्या उडून राख आणि दगडांच्या रूपात तो ज्वालामुखीतून स्फोटाने बाहेर फेकला जातो.

पृथ्वीचं कवच मोठमोठ्या [[tectonic-plates|भूपट्टांनी]] बनलेलं आहे. बहुतेक ज्वालामुखी तिथे तयार होतात, जिथे दोन भूपट्ट एकमेकांपासून दूर सरकतात किंवा एक भूपट्ट दुसऱ्याच्या खाली जातो. हवाईसारखे काही ज्वालामुखी [[mantle|प्रावरणातल्या]] अतितप्त जागांवर, म्हणजे ‘हॉट स्पॉट’वर बसलेले आहेत.

पृथ्वीवरच्या जागृत ज्वालामुखींपैकी सुमारे तीन-चतुर्थांश प्रशांत महासागराला वेढून आहेत. घोड्याच्या नालेच्या आकाराच्या या पट्ट्याला अग्निवलय (रिंग ऑफ फायर) म्हणतात. तो न्यूझीलंड आणि इंडोनेशियापासून जपान, अलास्का आणि अँडीज पर्वतांपर्यंत पसरला आहे. तिथे महासागराखालचे भूपट्ट इतर भूपट्टांच्या खाली जातात आणि खाली जाताना वितळतात. [[@iceland|आइसलँड]] अशा एका सागरी डोंगररांगेवर वसलं आहे, जिथे दोन भूपट्ट एकमेकांपासून दूर सरकत आहेत.

इसवी सन 79 मध्ये इटलीतल्या व्हेसुव्हियस पर्वताने [[@pompeii|पॉम्पेई]] हे रोमन शहर राखेखाली गाडलं. त्या राखेने रस्ते, भट्ट्यांमधले पाव आणि भिंतींवरची चित्रं जशीच्या तशी जपली. त्यामुळे रोमन लोकांचं रोजचं आयुष्य आपल्याला एखाद्या फोटोसारखं दिसतं.

एप्रिल 1815 मध्ये इंडोनेशियातल्या तंबोरा पर्वताचा उद्रेक झाला. नोंदलेल्या इतिहासातला हा सर्वांत मोठा उद्रेक. त्याची राख आणि वायू जगभर पसरले आणि हवामान थंड झालं. 1816 मध्ये युरोप आणि उत्तर अमेरिकेत पिकं हातची गेली, आणि लोक त्या वर्षाला ‘उन्हाळा नसलेलं वर्ष’ म्हणू लागले.

18 मे 1980 रोजी अमेरिकेतल्या वॉशिंग्टन राज्यातल्या माउंट सेंट हेलेन्सची एका प्रचंड आडव्या स्फोटात एक बाजूच उडून गेली. काही मिनिटांत पर्वताची उंची सुमारे 400 मीटरने कमी झाली. शास्त्रज्ञ कित्येक आठवडे त्याच्यावर लक्ष ठेवून होते आणि त्यांनी तो भाग बंद केला होता. त्यामुळे अनेकांचे प्राण वाचले.

उद्रेक धोकादायक असू शकतात, पण ज्वालामुखीच्या राखेपासून पृथ्वीवरची काही सर्वांत [[fertile|सुपीक]] माती तयार होते, आणि ज्वालामुखींनी अनेक बेटं उभी केली आहेत.

[[@bali|इंडोनेशियातल्या]] जावासारख्या ठिकाणी लाखो शेतकरी जागृत ज्वालामुखींच्या उतारांवर राहतात, कारण तिथली माती खूप सुपीक आहे. आइसलँड जमिनीखालच्या ज्वालामुखीच्या उष्णतेने घरं उबदार ठेवतो आणि वीज तयार करतो. आणि [[@hawaii-islands|हवाई]] अजूनही वाढतंय, एकेका लाव्हा प्रवाहाने.

text: India's marine parks are protected areas in the sea, set up to keep coral reefs, seagrass beds, mangroves and sea creatures safe. They work like [[@national-parks|national parks]] on land, but much of what they protect is underwater.

India has a long coastline, more than 11,000 km including its islands by a 2024 measurement, and several marine national parks and [[sanctuary|sanctuaries]]. The best known are the Gulf of Kachchh in Gujarat, the Gulf of Mannar in Tamil Nadu and the Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park in the Andaman Islands.
Inside them, rules limit fishing, mining and building. Some zones are open to visitors, who can snorkel, take glass-bottomed boat rides or walk on reefs at low tide.

sec.t:
In 1982 the Gulf of Kachchh, on Gujarat's coast, became India's first marine national park. It covers dozens of islands and reefs, along with mangrove forests and mudflats.

The water here is warm and full of [[nutrient|nutrients]], but also murky and salty, so its corals are tough. At low tide the sea pulls far back, and visitors at places such as Narara can walk across the exposed reef with a guide. Small octopuses, [[@ocean-pufferfish|pufferfish]], sea cucumbers and colourful sea slugs hide in the pools.

sec.h: Gulf of Mannar and the dugongs
sec.t:
Between India and Sri Lanka lies the Gulf of Mannar. In 1986 a chain of 21 small islands off the Tamil Nadu coast, along with the shallow sea around them, became a marine national park. Two of those islands have since sunk below the waves, worn away after years of coral mining nearby.

Coral reefs ring the islands. Sea turtles, dolphins and hundreds of kinds of fish live here. So do some of India's last dugongs, large slow sea [[mammal|mammals]] related to elephants rather than whales. They graze on seagrass meadows on the sea floor.

Dugongs are now rare in India. In 2022 Tamil Nadu set up India's first Dugong Conservation Reserve in nearby Palk Bay, to protect the seagrass they depend on.

{{story:coral-bleaching}}

The [[@andaman|Andaman and Nicobar Islands]] have some of India's clearest water and richest [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]]. The Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park, near Wandoor on South Andaman, was declared in 1983. It protects 15 islands and their reefs.

Visitors take boats out to islands such as Jolly Buoy and Red Skin, where they can snorkel over branching corals and see parrotfish, clownfish and giant clams. To protect the reef, plastic bottles and bags are not allowed on Jolly Buoy island.

The Andamans also have Rani Jhansi Marine National Park, which protects mangroves, beaches and reefs around Ritchie's Archipelago.

Some marine sanctuaries protect beaches as much as water. At Gahirmatha in Odisha, hundreds of thousands of olive ridley [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]] sometimes come ashore over a few nights to lay eggs. This mass nesting is called an arribada, a Spanish word meaning "arrival".

During the nesting season, fishing close to shore is banned, because turtles get caught in nets.

Fences can't keep trawlers out of the sea. Marine parks rely on patrol boats, local rules and the help of fishing families who live alongside them.

Warming seas are a bigger threat. When the water stays too hot for too long, corals lose the tiny [[algae|algae]] that live inside them and turn white. This bleaching has hit reefs in the Gulf of Mannar, Lakshadweep and the Andamans several times since 1998.

Other countries face the same challenge. Australia's [[@great-barrier-reef|Great Barrier Reef]] is a marine park too, and in the USA, Hawaii's Papahānaumokuākea is one of the largest protected ocean areas in the world. In both places, as in India, scientists are learning which reefs can recover.

sec.h: Why low sounds travel so far
sec.t:
Low-pitched sounds lose less energy than high ones as they travel through air, and they bend around trees and hills more easily. On a calm evening, an elephant's rumble can carry for several kilometres across a [[savanna|savanna]] or forest. [[@whale-songs|Blue whales]] use the same trick in the ocean.

A rumble also shakes the ground. Elephants are so heavy that their calls, and even their footsteps, send tiny vibrations through the soil. These ground waves move a bit like very faint [[@earthquakes|earthquake]] waves, and they can sometimes travel further than the sound in the air.

Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell, an American [[biologist|biologist]], noticed wild elephants in Namibia sometimes froze, leaned forward and lifted a foot, as if listening. She and her team played recorded warning calls through the ground. The elephants grew alert and bunched together, even though the sound in the air was barely there.

Elephant feet and trunk tips are packed with nerve endings that sense pressure and vibration. Bones may carry the vibrations up to the [[@ears-hear|ear]] too. Scientists still don't know exactly how far elephants can "hear" this way, or how often they use it in daily life.

Elephant rumbles carry meaning. Some say "let's go", some greet a returning friend, and some warn of danger. A study of African elephants in Kenya found that females recognised the calls of around 100 other elephants, and reacted differently to friends and strangers. A 2024 study suggested that wild African elephants may even use name-like calls for particular members of their family.

Asian elephants have their own sounds. Besides rumbles and trumpets, they make high squeaks and chirps, a little like a bird.

India's wild elephants live mainly in the forests of the Western Ghats, the north-east and the eastern and central states, with Karnataka holding the most. Project Elephant began in 1992 to protect them and the corridors they use to travel between forests.

Those journeys sometimes bring elephants into farms and villages, where they can damage crops and homes, and both people and elephants get hurt. Understanding how elephants talk and find each other may one day help warn villages before a herd arrives. Like [[@crow-smart|crows]], elephants have long memories, and herds follow old routes their grandmothers knew.

text: When animal dung rots in a sealed tank with no air, tiny living things called [[@microbes-friendly|microbes]] eat it. As they feed, they give off a mix of gases called biogas. More than half of it is methane, the same gas that makes up most natural gas. Methane burns.

So a farming family with a few [[@cows-india|cows]] can mix their dung with water, pour it into an underground tank, and pipe the gas to a stove in the kitchen. It lights with a match and cooks dal and rotis like the gas from a cylinder. What comes out of the other end of the tank is a soft slurry, which goes onto the fields as [[fertiliser|fertiliser]].

st.reveal: Microbes that can't live with oxygen break the dung down slowly. As they feed, they give off methane and carbon dioxide. The farmer's job is mainly to keep them fed and warm.

sec.t:
The [[microbe|microbes]] doing the work are called anaerobic, which means "without air". Oxygen harms them. That's why the tank has to be sealed.

They work in teams. Some break the dung into simpler stuff, like sugars. Others turn that into [[acid|acids]]. The last group, which are among the oldest kinds of life on Earth, turn those acids into methane. A cow's stomach holds the same kind of microbes, which is partly why cows burp out methane.

They like warmth. A tank works well in a hot Indian summer and slows down in a cold winter, the way [[@compost|compost]] does.

{{story:microbes-friendly}}

A common Indian design looks like a buried dome of brick or concrete. Fresh dung and water go in through one pipe, a bit every day. The gas collects at the top of the dome and pushes out through a thin pipe to the kitchen. The used slurry flows out of a second opening into a pit.

India has built family biogas plants since the 1980s. China did the same on an even larger scale, with millions of rural families building tanks from the 1970s onwards. About 50 lakh have been installed under the national programme. A family plant can often supply most of a small household's cooking, though it needs a steady supply of dung and water to keep going.

Running one takes care. If the plant isn't fed every day, the microbes go hungry and the gas dwindles. Government audits have found that some village plants stopped working because of leaks, too few cattle or nobody nearby who could fix them, so newer schemes train local mechanics.

In many villages, people still cook on wood, crop waste or dried dung cakes burned in a chulha. The smoke fills kitchens, and the World Health Organization lists smoky indoor cooking as a big cause of lung disease, especially for women and young children. A biogas flame gives off almost no smoke.

It also helps with waste. Dung left in heaps gives off methane straight into the air, where it traps heat much more strongly than [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Burning that methane as fuel turns it into carbon dioxide, which is less harmful, and saves wood and [[@cooking-gas|cooking gas]] at the same time.

Biogas works on more than dung. Kitchen scraps, sewage, crop stalks and market waste can all feed the microbes. Some Indian cities run plants on vegetable waste from markets. In the USA, large dairy farms use covered ponds to trap gas from manure, and old rubbish dumps are piped to collect the methane seeping out of them.

Cleaned and squeezed into tanks, biogas can even run buses and cars. India has a scheme to build plants that sell this compressed biogas like any other fuel. It is a slightly odd thought: one day the bus to school might run partly on cow dung.

text: An echo is sound that has bounced off something and come back to you. Sound travels through air as a wave, a ripple of squeezed and stretched air spreading out from its source. When that wave hits a large, hard surface, like a cliff, a wall or the inside of a dome, much of it bounces back, the way a ball bounces off a wall.

If the surface is far enough away, the bounced sound arrives a moment after the original, and you hear it as a separate copy of your voice. Soft surfaces like curtains, grass and snow soak up sound instead of reflecting it, so they make poor echoes.

sec.t:
Sound in air travels about 343 metres every second, roughly the length of three football fields. That sounds fast, but your brain can notice gaps of about a tenth of a second. Anything closer together blends into one sound.

In a tenth of a second, sound goes about 34 metres. Since an echo has to travel there and back, you need to be at least about 17 metres from a wall to hear a clear, separate echo. Closer than that, the reflection arrives too soon. It still happens, but it mixes with the original and just makes the sound richer, like singing in a bathroom. That blurred, lingering sound is called reverberation.

Some animals use echoes to find their way. [[@bats-fly|Bats]] send out high-pitched calls, usually too high for us to hear, and listen to the echoes. From how long each echo takes and how it sounds, a bat can tell where a moth is, how big it is and which way it's flying. This is called [[echolocation|echolocation]].

Dolphins and some whales do the same underwater with clicks. A few birds that live in dark caves, such as oilbirds in South America and some swiftlets in Asia, use simpler clicks to avoid hitting walls.

People copied the animals. Ships use sonar, sending pulses of sound down into the sea and timing the echoes to measure depth. This is how scientists [[@ocean-floor-maps|mapped the ocean floor]], finding underwater mountain ranges longer than any on land. Doctors use [[ultrasound|ultrasound]], very high-pitched sound, to see babies growing inside their mothers and to check hearts and kidneys.

Concert halls are designed with echoes in mind. Architects shape walls and ceilings, and add soft panels, so that music sounds full but not muddy. Too many echoes, and every note smears into the next. Too few, and a hall sounds dead, as in a [[@soundproofing|soundproofed]] studio.

text: A hologram is a kind of picture that captures depth. When you move your head, you can see around the objects in it, as if they were really there behind the glass. An ordinary photo can't do that. It stays flat whichever way you look.

The difference is in what each one records. A photo records how bright and what colour the light is at each point. A hologram also records the shape of the light waves, which carry information about how far away each part of the scene was. When light shines on the hologram later, those waves are rebuilt, and your eyes see the scene in three dimensions.

sec.t:
Light travels as waves, with peaks and dips, a bit like ripples on a pond. When two sets of ripples cross, they make a pattern. Where peaks meet peaks, the water rises higher. Where peaks meet dips, they cancel out.

To make a hologram, scientists split a beam of laser light in two. One beam lights up the object, then bounces off it onto a special photographic plate. The other beam goes straight to the plate. The two beams overlap, making a fine pattern of light and dark stripes, far too small to see. That pattern is the hologram. When the right light shines through it later, the pattern bends the light into the same waves that came off the object.

sec.h: An idea waiting for the laser

sec.t:
You've probably held a hologram today. The shiny, rainbow-coloured stickers on bank cards, passports, concert tickets, medicine packets and some brand-name products are holograms. They're very hard to copy with an ordinary printer or photocopier, so they help show something is genuine.

These security holograms are made differently from laboratory ones. They work in ordinary light, and their rainbow colours shift as you tilt them. They're pressed into thin metal foil like tiny grooves, millions at a time.

In the film [[@star-wars-effect|Star Wars]] (1977), a small robot projects a glowing, flickering message from Princess Leia into thin air. It became the most famous "hologram" in the world, and inspired scientists and engineers for decades. Real holograms can't float in empty air like that, because the light has to come from a surface.

So what about the singers who appear on stage at concerts, sometimes years after they've died? These usually use a trick called Pepper's ghost. A bright video is shown on a screen hidden below or above the stage and reflected in a sheet of clear glass or film angled towards the audience. The reflection seems to float. The trick was made famous by the scientist John Henry Pepper in a London show in 1862, to make a ghost appear in a play, and [[@theatre|theatres]] soon copied it.

text: A returning boomerang comes back because it does two things at once. It spins very fast, and each of its arms is shaped like a little aeroplane wing. As it whirls through the air, the arms make lift, a sideways push, just as wings do.

Here is the clever part. The arm at the top of the spin is moving forward through the air faster than the arm at the bottom, so it makes more lift. That uneven push tries to tip the boomerang over. But because it is spinning, it doesn't tip. Instead it slowly turns, like a bicycle leaning into a bend, and curves around in a big circle back towards you.

sec.t:
Look at a boomerang's arms from the side. One edge is rounded and one is thin, and the top is more curved than the bottom. That is an aerofoil, the same shape as the wing of a plane. When air flows over it, it creates lift, which is explained in [[@airplanes-fly|how aeroplanes fly]].

A boomerang is thrown almost upright, so its lift pushes sideways rather than up. The thrower adds a hard flick of the wrist, giving it perhaps ten spins every second. Wind matters too. Throwers usually face the breeze and aim a little to the right of it, so the wind helps carry the boomerang round.

Spinning objects behave strangely when you push them. Push the top of a spinning top and it doesn't fall, it swings around. Scientists call this precession.

The faster top arm of the boomerang always makes more lift than the slower bottom arm. That tries to tip the boomerang onto its side. Precession turns that tip into a steady turn. The boomerang curves left (for a right-handed thrower), circling round in a loop that can be 20–30 m wide, about the length of a cricket pitch.

Distance throwers use special boomerangs that loop out more than 100 m and still return, further than the length of a football field. Others are built to hover and drift down slowly, staying in the air for well over a minute.

Aboriginal Australians have made boomerangs for many thousands of years. Most were heavy, nearly straight hunting sticks, sometimes called kylies, which flew straight and hit hard. Lighter, curved returning boomerangs were used for sport, for practice and to scare birds into nets.

India had throwing sticks too. In Tamil Nadu, the valari was a curved stick of wood or iron thrown in hunting and battle. Some people say certain valaris could return, but most were meant to hit and stay down.

In March 2008, Japanese astronaut Takao Doi tested a small boomerang aboard the International [[@space-station|Space Station]]. In the station everything floats, so nothing pulled it towards the floor, but there was air inside. The boomerang curved round and came back to his hand.

That shows [[gravity|gravity]] isn't what brings it home. Air and spin do all the work. A boomerang is really a spinning pair of wings. Its closest cousin may be the tilted wing of a [[@how-kites-fly-physics|kite]], which needs a string to stay up, while a boomerang needs nothing but a good throw.

The moulds pass through hot ovens to dry and toughen the rubber. Spinning brushes roll the open end into the neat lip you put your mouth on. Then jets of air or water pop the finished balloons off the moulds, and they are washed, dried and packed. A big machine can make many thousands an hour.

sec.t:
Latex comes from the rubber tree, which first grew in the Amazon rainforest. Workers make a slanting cut in the bark early in the morning, and a white, sticky liquid drips into a cup. It is not sap but a defence the tree uses to seal wounds.

India is one of the world's big natural rubber producers, and most of it comes from [[@kerala|Kerala]], where rubber plantations cover the hills. Much of India's rubber goes into tyres, but some ends up as gloves and balloons.

Raw latex goes soft when warm and brittle when cold. In 1839, the American Charles Goodyear found that heating rubber with sulphur made it strong and stretchy, a process called vulcanisation, part of the story of [[@accident-vulcanised-rubber|accidental inventions]].

Before rubber, people made balloons from animal bladders and intestines. Children in many places played with blown-up pig bladders.

In 1824, the scientist Michael Faraday made the first rubber balloons at the Royal Institution in London. He pressed two sheets of rubber together, with flour inside so they wouldn't stick, and filled them with hydrogen for experiments. A year later, a company began selling kits so people could make their own toy balloons.

The modern shape came in the 1930s, when Neil Tillotson in the USA dipped moulds into liquid latex. One of his first balloons had a cat's face with two ears.

{{story:hot-air-balloons}}

A balloon full of your breath sinks, because breath is a little heavier than air. Fill it with helium, which is lighter than air, and it floats up, pushed by the heavier air around it, the same way a cork bobs up in water.

But helium [[atom|atoms]] are tiny. They slip through the gaps in a latex skin, and most helium balloons sag within a day. Foil balloons, made of nylon coated with a metal layer, hold helium for a week or more. That's why they are popular for birthdays.

Helium itself is precious. It is mined from underground gas fields, and doctors need it to cool MRI scanners. Some scientists argue it is too valuable to float away at parties.

Not all balloons are toys. Weather services release [[@weather-balloons|weather balloons]] twice a day around the world, including from India Meteorological Department stations. They carry instruments up to around 30 km, where the balloon swells to the size of a small house and bursts.

Doctors use tiny balloons inside blood vessels to open blockages near the heart. And in the Second World War, armies built fake tanks out of inflatable rubber to fool enemy spies. Those balloon tanks were part of a long history of disguise and trickery among [[@spies-history|spies]].

text: There are a few main ways to build a tunnel. For shallow tunnels, workers can dig a trench, build the tunnel inside it and then cover it over. This is called cut-and-cover, and many older underground railways were built like this.

Through hard [[@rocks-types|rock]], crews drill holes, fill them with explosives and blast the rock away, a few metres at a time. Then they clear the rubble and strengthen the walls with steel and concrete.

For long tunnels through softer rock or under cities and rivers, engineers use [[@extreme-biggest-machines|a tunnel boring machine]]. Its front is a giant spinning wheel covered in cutters that grinds through the ground. Behind it, the machine fits curved concrete pieces into rings that become the tunnel's walls. It is a moving factory, often longer than a train.

sec.t:
In 1825, the engineer Marc Brunel began digging a tunnel under the River Thames in [[@london|London]]. Nobody had ever tunnelled under a big, busy river before. The soft, wet mud kept threatening to cave in.

Brunel had studied the shipworm, which bores through wood while protecting itself with its shell. He designed an iron shield for his workers to stand inside as they dug, inching forward bit by bit. The river burst in more than once, and his young son, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, nearly drowned. The tunnel finally opened in 1843. It still carries [[@trains-how|trains]] today, and nearly every soft-ground tunnel since has used a shield.

Mountains bring other problems: hard rock, heat deep inside, water gushing from cracks and, sometimes, rocks that shift. [[@extreme-longest-tunnels|The Gotthard Base Tunnel]] in [[@switzerland|Switzerland]], opened in 2016, runs about 57 kilometres beneath the Alps. It is the longest railway tunnel in the world, and in places there are more than 2 kilometres of rock overhead.

In the Himalaya, [[@india-wonder-atal-tunnel|the Atal Tunnel]] near Manali opened in 2020. It is about 9 kilometres long and lies above 3,000 metres. It lets traffic avoid the Rohtang Pass, which is often closed by snow for months. The young [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]] are still rising and full of cracked rock, which makes tunnelling there especially hard.

Long tunnels need fresh air, so giant fans push stale air out and pull clean air in. They need lights, drainage pumps and escape routes. The Channel Tunnel actually has three tunnels: two for trains and a smaller service tunnel between them for workers and emergencies.

Tunnel crews have old traditions too. In many countries, a tunnel boring machine is given a woman's name before it starts digging. In Europe, a small statue of Saint Barbara, the protector of miners, is often placed at the tunnel entrance. Indian crews often hold a puja before the cutters first bite into the rock.

text: A comic tells a story in a sequence of pictures, usually arranged in boxes called panels, with words in speech balloons and captions. Making one is often a team job. A writer plans the story and the words. A penciller draws the pictures. An inker goes over the [[@pencils|pencil lines]] in black ink. A colourist adds colour, and a letterer adds the words and sound effects.
Some artists do all of these jobs themselves. Today many comics are drawn on computers and tablets, but the steps are much the same as they were with pencils, brushes and paper.

Nothing, the panels are unrelated

st.reveal: The gap between panels is called the gutter. Readers fill it in automatically, imagining the action that connects two pictures. Comic artists rely on this to tell stories quickly.

Comics are written for every age. Some graphic novels deal with history and serious subjects. Art Spiegelman's Maus, about the Holocaust, won a special Pulitzer Prize in 1992.

sec.t:
A comic usually begins as a script. The writer describes each page: how many panels, what happens in each, and what everyone says. A page with lots of small panels feels busy and fast. A single huge panel makes a big moment, like a giant explosion or a hero's arrival, feel important.

Next, the artist makes rough sketches, called thumbnails, to plan where characters stand and where the balloons will go. Then come the careful pencils, the bold ink lines and the colours. Lettering comes last, so the words never cover anything important.

In comics, words are part of the picture. Speech balloons have a tail pointing to the speaker. A cloud-shaped bubble shows thoughts. Spiky balloons show shouting, and tiny letters show whispering.

Sound effects like CRASH, WHOOSH or DHISHOOM are drawn as big, shaped letters that look like the noise. Even the style of lettering can tell you who is speaking: a robot might talk in square letters, a ghost in wobbly ones. Long before speech balloons, people told stories in picture sequences on temple walls and in [[@art-cheriyal|scrolls]], a bit like the way [[@writing-began|writing began]] with pictures.

Newspaper comic strips became popular in the United States in the 1890s. In 1938, two young men from Ohio, Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, published the first Superman story, and comic books about [[@superheroes-history|superheroes]] took off.

In Japan, manga grew hugely after the Second World War, led by artists like Osamu Tezuka, creator of *Astro Boy*. Manga are read right to left and are often printed in black and white, which lets artists draw hundreds of pages quickly. Many become [[@studio-ghibli|anime]].

In 1967 Anant Pai started [[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]], comics that retold stories from the epics, history and [[@indian-folk-tales|folk tales]]. He reportedly got the idea after noticing that children on a TV quiz could answer questions about Greek myths but not about Indian ones. Generations of Indian children learned the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the lives of historical figures from these comics.

The cartoonist Pran created Chacha Chaudhary in 1971, a clever old man whose brain works faster than a computer, with his giant friend Sabu from Jupiter. *[[@tinkle|Tinkle]]* magazine followed in 1980, with characters like Suppandi. Today Indian artists also publish [[@graphic-novels|graphic novels]] and web comics on phones, and you can read about them in [[@comics-india|India's favourite comic heroes]].

text: Georgia O'Keeffe was an American painter who lived from 1887 to 1986. She is famous for enormous close-up paintings of flowers, for glowing pictures of the New Mexico desert, and for bleached animal skulls floating in the sky. She is often called one of the founders of modern art in America.

She painted in a clean, simple way, with smooth colours and crisp edges. Many of her pictures look partly real and partly abstract, meaning built from shapes and colours rather than exact details. She worked for more than seven decades and kept making art even after her eyesight began to fail.

Cactus spines

st.reveal: She collected cow and horse skulls, pelvis bones and antlers from the desert. To her they were beautiful shapes, not gloomy symbols. She painted them floating against hills and wide blue skies.

sec.h: A farm girl who wanted to be an artist
sec.t:
O'Keeffe grew up on a dairy farm in Wisconsin. By the age of ten, she had decided to be an artist, which was a bold plan for a girl at the time. She studied in Chicago and New York, then worked as an art teacher, including in the dusty plains of Texas, where the big skies stayed with her for life.

In 1915 she made a set of charcoal drawings that looked like nothing else: swirling lines and shapes, with no people or objects. A friend showed them to Alfred Stieglitz, a famous photographer who ran a gallery in [[@new-york|New York]]. He exhibited them in 1916. The two later married, and Stieglitz took hundreds of [[@photography-art|photographs]] of her.

sec.h: Flowers the size of a window
sec.t:
In the 1920s O'Keeffe began painting single flowers, so close and so large that they filled the whole canvas. A petunia, an iris or a calla lily became as big as a window. She explained that people rush past flowers without seeing them, so she would paint them too big to ignore.

Critics wrote a lot about what the flowers "meant". O'Keeffe often grew tired of this. She said she was simply painting what she saw. In 2014, one of these pictures, *Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1*, sold for 44.4 million dollars, setting a record at the time for a work by a woman at auction.

Living in New York in the late 1920s, she painted the city too. From a high apartment, she looked down at [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]] rising around her and painted them at night, glowing with lights, or with the sun flaring behind them. She later said that some male artists told her only men should paint the city. She painted it anyway.

{{story:skyscrapers}}

In 1929 O'Keeffe first spent a summer in New Mexico, and the landscape changed her life. She called it "the faraway". There were red and yellow cliffs, a flat-topped mountain called the Pedernal and a sky that seemed to go on forever.

For years she spent summers there and winters in New York. After Stieglitz died, she moved to New Mexico for good in 1949, living in two houses at Abiquiú and Ghost Ranch. She walked the [[@deserts-world|deserts]] collecting bones and stones and painted them against the hills.

O'Keeffe began flying around the world in her seventies, visiting places from Peru to India and Japan. Looking down from aeroplane windows, she saw rivers winding like ribbons and clouds lying below her like a floor. These became new paintings. *Sky Above Clouds IV*, finished in 1965, is more than 7 metres wide and now hangs at the Art Institute of Chicago.

In her eighties her eyesight weakened, and she worked on pottery and drawings with help from an assistant. She died in Santa Fe in 1986, aged 98. The Georgia O'Keeffe Museum there opened in 1997, one of the first museums in the USA devoted to a single woman artist. Like [[@frida-kahlo|Frida Kahlo]] in Mexico, she showed a whole generation that a woman could be a great modern painter.

text: Indian theatre is a huge family of traditions, some ancient and some brand new. It ranges from Sanskrit plays more than 1,500 years old to all-night folk performances in village squares, and from modern plays in city auditoriums to [[@street-theatre|street plays]] on a corner.

Much Indian theatre mixes acting with music, dance and song. Performers often tell stories from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Puranas, as well as local legends. Actors use detailed hand gestures, facial expressions and painted make-up. The aim is often less about making things look realistic and more about making the audience feel deeply. The oldest guide to all this is the Natyashastra.

st.reveal: Rasa means juice or flavour. The Natyashastra says a good performance lets the audience "taste" an emotion such as love, courage or wonder, the way a cook blends spices into a flavour.

d.try: Play the navarasa game. One person shows an emotion using only their face and hands and no words. Choose from love, laughter, sorrow, anger, courage, fear, disgust, wonder or peace. Everyone else guesses which one. Then try showing the same emotion with only your eyes.

Some European scholars in the 1800s suggested this, but there's little evidence for it. Most historians now see Indian theatre as growing out of India's own traditions of ritual, storytelling, music and dance.

sec.t:
The Natyashastra is credited to a sage called Bharata Muni. Scholars date it to somewhere between about 200 BCE and 200 CE. It is an enormous book covering almost everything about putting on a play: acting, stage design, costumes, make-up, music and dance.

It describes how to show emotions with every part of the body, down to the eyebrows and eyelids. Its central idea is rasa, the "flavour" an audience tastes when a performance works. The Natyashastra describes eight rasas, including love, humour, sorrow and wonder. Later writers added a ninth, peace, making the navarasa, or nine rasas, still taught today.

Classical Sanskrit drama reached a high point with [[@kalidasa|Kalidasa]], who probably lived around the 4th or 5th century CE. His play Abhijnanashakuntalam tells of King Dushyanta, who falls in love with Shakuntala in a forest hermitage and then forgets her because of a curse. When it was translated into English and German around 1790, writers in Europe were deeply impressed.

Sanskrit plays usually ended happily. The Natyashastra advised against showing death on stage, so tragedy, in the Greek sense, was rare.

In Kerala, a form called Kutiyattam has kept Sanskrit theatre alive for centuries. Performers might spend a whole night acting out a single scene in great detail. UNESCO recognised it in 2001.

{{story:kalidasa}}

Almost every part of India has its own folk theatre. [[@yakshagana|Yakshagana]] from coastal Karnataka has huge headdresses, drums and all-night shows. Kerala's [[@kathakali|Kathakali]] uses brightly painted faces and dance to tell epic stories. Bengal has jatra, travelling troupes who perform under the open sky. Maharashtra has tamasha, full of song and comedy. Uttar Pradesh has nautanki, and Gujarat has bhavai.

Ramlila, a retelling of the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] staged before Dussehra, is performed in towns and villages across north India. In Ramnagar, near Varanasi, it lasts about a month and moves around the town, with different neighbourhoods acting as different places in the story.

In the 1800s, Parsi theatre companies in Bombay put on lively shows with songs, painted backdrops and stage tricks. Many early film actors and writers came from this world, and you can see its style in early [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] films.

After independence, the National School of Drama opened in Delhi in 1959. Playwrights such as Girish Karnad, Vijay Tendulkar and Badal Sircar wrote powerful plays in Kannada, Marathi and Bengali. Habib Tanvir worked with folk actors from Chhattisgarh, and his play Charandas Chor, about an honest thief, toured the world.

In Mumbai, the actor Shashi Kapoor and his wife Jennifer Kendal opened Prithvi Theatre in 1978, named after his father Prithviraj Kapoor, who had run a touring theatre company. It's a small theatre where audiences sit very close to the actors.

In the 1800s, some European scholars suggested Indian theatre began when [[@alexander-india|Alexander]]'s Greek armies arrived. Most historians today reject that idea. Indian drama seems to have grown from its own roots: temple [[ritual|rituals]], storytellers, music and dance. Whatever its beginnings, it is still growing. Somewhere in India tonight, a curtain is opening, or a drum is calling a village to gather.

text: A puppet is a figure that a person moves to tell a story. It comes alive through movement, voice and the audience's imagination. Puppeteers practise for years to make a figure of wood, cloth or leather seem to breathe, think and feel.

There are four main kinds. String puppets, or marionettes, hang from strings tied to a control. Glove puppets fit over the hand. Rod puppets are moved by sticks from below or behind. Shadow puppets are flat figures held between a lamp and a screen, so the audience sees only their shadows. India has all four, and so do many other countries.

options.t: The leather is scraped thin and dyed, so light shines through it like stained glass
Coloured lights are pointed at the audience

st.reveal: In Andhra's tholu bommalata, puppet makers scrape animal hide until it is thin enough to be see-through, then dye it and punch tiny holes for patterns. With a lamp behind, the puppets glow in colour.

sec.t:
The secret of a good puppet show is that small movements suggest a lot. A slight tilt of the head looks like curiosity. A slump of the shoulders looks like sadness. Our brains are very good at reading feelings from body language, even in a block of wood.

Puppeteers also make sure the puppet seems to look at whatever it is talking to, and pauses before it speaks, as if it is thinking. Together with a good voice, this makes the audience forget, for a while, that someone is holding the strings.

Shadow puppetry is found from India to [[@bali|Indonesia]] and China. In Andhra Pradesh, tholu bommalata puppets are made from animal hide, scraped so thin it lets light through, then dyed in bright colours. Some are life-sized. Behind a white screen, an oil lamp or bulb makes them glow.

Shows often tell stories from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] and can last all night. [[@karnataka|Karnataka]] has a similar tradition called togalu gombeyata, and [[@kerala|Kerala]] has tolpava koothu, performed in temples. In Indonesia, wayang kulit shadow puppetry is listed by UNESCO as world cultural heritage.

In Japan, Bunraku puppet theatre grew up in Osaka more than 300 years ago. Its puppets are more than a metre tall. One senior puppeteer moves the head and right arm, a second moves the left arm, and a third moves the feet. Junior puppeteers often train for years on the feet alone before they are allowed to move a head.

The puppeteers stand on stage in full view, often dressed in black. Yet after a few minutes, audiences stop seeing them and watch only the puppet. A narrator chants all the voices, accompanied by a three-stringed instrument called the shamisen. It is a form of [[@theatre|theatre]] for adults, full of love stories and tragedy.

In the United States, Jim Henson created the Muppets, starting with a TV show in 1955. In 1969 his characters joined *[[@sesame-street|Sesame Street]]*, which taught letters and numbers to millions of children around the world. India had its own version, *Galli Galli Sim Sim*, from 2006.

Puppets also live on in films through stop-motion, where puppets are moved a tiny bit between each photograph, as in [[@animation-how|animation]]. Many traditional Indian puppeteers struggle to make a living today, but festivals and schools are working to keep their skills alive.

text: Free speech is the right to say what you think, write it, draw it or share it, without being punished by the government. It covers speeches, books, newspapers, films, art, protests and posts online. It also includes the right to criticise those in power.

[[democracy|Democracies]] treat it as basic, because people can't choose their leaders well without hearing different ideas. But no country allows every kind of speech. Threats, fraud and lies that harm someone's reputation are limited almost everywhere. The big arguments are about where else to draw the line.

myth: Free speech means you can say anything, anywhere, with no consequences.

Free speech protects you from being punished by the government for your views, within limits. It does not stop others from disagreeing, and most countries still ban things like threats, fraud and lies that damage someone's reputation.

sec.t:
The US [[@us-constitution|Constitution]]'s First Amendment, added in 1791, says Congress shall make "no law" limiting freedom of speech or of the press. American courts read this very strongly. Even hateful speech is usually protected, unless it is meant to cause immediate violence.

India's [[@constitution|Constitution]] guarantees freedom of speech and expression in Article 19. But it also allows "reasonable restrictions" for reasons such as public order, decency, the security of the state and friendly relations with other countries. Courts decide what counts as reasonable. Many other democracies, like Germany, ban certain kinds of hate speech outright.

India's limits were debated from the very start. In 1950, the Supreme Court sided with a magazine editor whose paper had been banned from Madras state. The next year, Parliament changed the Constitution in its [[@constitution-amendments|first-ever amendment]], adding public order and friendly relations with other countries to the list of allowed limits. At the world level, Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, agreed in 1948, says everyone has the right to "seek, receive and impart information and ideas".

In India, a section of the Information Technology Act once allowed arrests for online posts that were "grossly offensive" or caused "annoyance". People were arrested for social media comments, including two young women in Maharashtra in 2012 over a Facebook post and a "like".

In 2015, in a case brought by law student Shreya Singhal, the Supreme Court struck the section down. It ruled that the words were so vague that they could punish almost any opinion. Today, arguments continue about how [[@social-media|social media]] companies should handle false or hateful posts without silencing ordinary users.

Free speech protects unpopular ideas, because popular ones rarely need protecting. Many causes we now see as obviously right, like [[@womens-rights|votes for women]] and the end of slavery, began as opinions most people disliked.

It also lets citizens find out what governments are doing. A free press, using [[@journalism|journalism]] and records, can uncover mistakes and wrongdoing. Where speech is tightly controlled, only one side can be heard, and [[@propaganda|propaganda]] fills the gap.

Free speech works best alongside listening. You can disagree strongly with someone and still defend their right to speak.

text: Companies sell around the world by setting up shops, factories or partners in other countries, and by changing their products to suit local people. A company that does this is called a multinational.

Some open their own branches. Others let local business owners run shops under their name, which is called franchising. Many make things in one country, sell them in another and buy parts from a dozen more. Ships, planes, the internet and trade agreements tie it all together. The hard part is not getting the product there. It is persuading people in a new place, with different tastes, laws and languages, to want it.

sec.t:
When McDonald's opened its first Indian restaurant in Delhi in 1996, it knew a beef burger would not work. It invented new items: the McAloo Tikki, a spiced potato patty, and a chicken version of the Big Mac called the Maharaja Mac. Its kitchens keep vegetarian and non-vegetarian food apart.

Other companies do the same. KitKat in Japan comes in dozens of flavours, including green tea. Pizza chains in India add paneer and tandoori toppings. The idea is called localisation. A global brand keeps its name and logo but bends almost everything else. It's part of the long story of [[@fast-food-history|fast food]] spreading across the world.

Even names and adverts change. Some products are renamed so they are easy to say, or so they don't sound silly in the local language. Adverts swap faces, music and festivals. In India, many global brands launch their biggest campaigns around Diwali, while in the USA the busiest shopping season begins just after Thanksgiving.

Global companies are not all American or European. Tata, an Indian group, bought the British tea brand Tetley in 2000 and the car makers Jaguar and Land Rover in 2008. Indian software companies such as Infosys and TCS run computer systems for banks and shops across the world.

Smaller firms go global too. A craft business in Jaipur can sell block-printed cloth to buyers in Texas through a website. Selling abroad once needed offices in each country. Today, for some products, it needs a good website and a reliable courier. Some companies end up with more customers abroad than at home. Netflix, an American company, and Spotify, a Swedish one, both have most of their users outside their home countries.

Selling abroad brings headaches. Each country has its own taxes, safety rules and labelling laws. Money changes value, so a price that made sense last year might not this year. [[@advertising|Advertising]] has to work in new languages, and a joke or colour that feels friendly in one place can feel rude in another.

Big global companies also face criticism. Some are accused of pushing out small local shops, paying low wages in factories or avoiding taxes. Governments try to set rules so that their own businesses can compete fairly. Others argue that global companies bring jobs, cheaper goods and new ideas. Both views shape the laws countries write about trade.

text: Ancient India knew the rule, and wrote it down early. A Sanskrit text called the Baudhayana Sulba Sutra states it clearly. It is usually dated somewhere between about 800 and 500 BCE, around the time of [[@pythagoras|Pythagoras]] or before.

But "first" is tricky. Clay tablets from Babylon, from about 1800 BCE, already list number sets that fit the rule. And Baudhayana, like the Babylonians, gave the rule without the kind of step-by-step proof the Greeks later became known for. So the fair answer is that several ancient peoples knew it, and India's statement is one of the oldest and clearest.

sec.t:
During the [[@vedic-age|Vedic age]], important ceremonies needed fire altars built in exact shapes and sizes. Some were squares or [[@circles|circles]]. Others were shaped like birds, such as a falcon with outspread wings, made of hundreds of carefully cut bricks.

Getting the shape right mattered. Priests believed the [[ritual|ritual]] only worked if the altar was precise. So they needed ways to draw right angles, make a square with twice the area of another, or turn a square into a circle of the same area. The tools were simple: ropes and pegs. The word *sulba* itself means cord.

Baudhayana's Sulba Sutra is the oldest of several such texts. In one verse, it says roughly this: the rope stretched along the diagonal of a rectangle makes an area equal to the areas made by the two sides together. That is the same rule as a² + b² = c².

The text also gives triangles with whole-number sides that obey the rule, such as 3, 4 and 5, and 5, 12 and 13. Builders could use these to make perfect right angles with a knotted rope. Later Sulba Sutras by Apastamba and Katyayana repeat and extend these ideas.

The texts also explain how to turn one shape into another with the same area, for example a square into a rectangle, or two squares into one bigger square. Some even try to make a circle with the same area as a square. That cannot be done exactly, but their rope methods came close enough for a brick altar.

{{story:vedic-age}}

To make a square with double the area of another, you need a side that is the first side times the [[@square-roots|square root]] of 2. That number is about 1.41421356, and its digits never end or repeat.

Baudhayana's text gives a recipe: take 1, add a third, add a quarter of that third, then take away one thirty-fourth of that quarter. It comes to about 1.4142156. That is correct to five [[decimal|decimal]] places, close enough that a builder could never measure the difference with a rope.

People sometimes argue about who discovered the rule first, and the debate can get heated. Historians try to stick to the evidence. Babylonian tablets prove the rule was used there very early. The Sulba Sutras show it was understood independently in India. Chinese texts show it in China too.

What the Sulba Sutras show most clearly is how practical needs pushed maths forward. Priests wanted perfect altars, so they found reliable [[geometry|geometry]]. Centuries later, Indian mathematicians such as [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]] built on this tradition, working on astronomy, the number pi and much more. The rope-stretchers of the Vedic age were among the first in a long line.

text: Cricket is a game of numbers, and two of the most important are the average and the strike rate. A batting average tells you how many runs a batter scores, on average, each time they get out. A strike rate tells you how fast they score: how many runs they would make if they faced 100 balls.

Bowlers have their own numbers. A bowling average is the runs they give away for each wicket they take, so lower is better. An [[economy|economy]] rate is the runs they give away per over. Together, these numbers help selectors pick teams, captains plan tactics and fans argue about who is the greatest.

st.prompt: A batter scores 300 runs in 10 innings and is not out in 4 of them. What is their batting average?
st.reveal: The average divides runs by the number of times the batter was out, not by innings. They were out 10 − 4 = 6 times, so the average is 300 ÷ 6 = 50. Being not out helps an average a lot.

It is total runs divided by the number of times the batter was dismissed. Innings where the batter stayed not out add runs but don't add to the number you divide by, which is why some lower-order batters have surprisingly high averages.

sec.t:
The rule is simple: divide total runs by the number of times out. If a batter scores 450 runs and is dismissed 9 times, their average is 450 ÷ 9 = 50.

The tricky part is "not out". If a batter finishes an innings without being dismissed, their runs still count, but that innings is not added to the number you divide by. So two batters with the same runs and innings can have very different averages. This helps batters who often finish not out, and it is one reason averages should be read with care, a point made in many guides to [[@statistics-lies|statistics]].

sec.h: Strike rate and the T20 age
sec.t:
In a [[@test-cricket|Test match]], batting for a long time matters, so average is king. In shorter formats, speed matters too. A batter's strike rate is runs ÷ balls faced × 100. Score 30 runs off 20 balls and your strike rate is 150. Score 30 off 60 and it is 50.

In T20 leagues like the [[@ipl|IPL]], a strike rate of 150 or more is often seen as excellent, while in Test cricket many batters score at well under 60. A bowler's economy rate matters most in T20 too. Giving away 6 runs an over is very good, while 10 or more is expensive.

Bowlers also have a strike rate, but it means something different: the number of balls they bowl, on average, for each wicket. A bowler who takes 10 wickets in 300 balls has a strike rate of 30. For a bowler, unlike a batter, a lower strike rate is better.

[[@sachin-tendulkar|Sachin Tendulkar]] holds the records for most runs in both Test cricket, with 15,921, and one-day internationals, with 18,426. His Test average was 53.78. But comparing players across eras is hard. Pitches, bats, rules, the number of matches played and the quality of opposing teams have all changed.

That is why [[@maths-sports-stats|statisticians invent new measures]], such as averages in matches a team won, or runs scored against the strongest bowlers. Numbers can settle some arguments, but in cricket they usually start a few more.

text: Shakuntala Devi was an Indian mathematician and performer who could do enormous calculations in her head faster than most people could type them into a machine. Newspapers called her the "human computer".

She toured the world from the 1950s onwards, solving problems shouted out by audiences at universities, schools and theatres. In 1980 she set a world record by multiplying two 13-digit numbers in 28 seconds. She also beat a computer in a contest in Dallas in 1977, finding the 23rd root of a 201-digit number. Later in life she wrote books to help children enjoy maths, arguing that numbers should be fun rather than frightening.

sec.t:
Shakuntala Devi was born in Bangalore, now [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]], on 4 November 1929. Her father performed in a [[@circus|circus]] as a trapeze artist and showman. When she was about three, he was teaching her card tricks and realised she was remembering every card and beating him.

The family was poor, and she never attended school regularly. Instead, her father took her on the road to show her skills. By the age of six she was performing calculations at the University of Mysore, and she was soon giving shows across India.

She never fully explained her methods. What is clear is that she practised with numbers every day from early childhood. In 1988, the American psychologist Arthur Jensen tested her at the University of California, Berkeley. He found she could find cube roots and other answers faster than he could copy down the question.

Scientists who study mental calculation think experts like her use a huge store of number facts in [[@memory|memory]], so they don't have to work out small steps again. They also break big problems into chunks in clever ways. Mental [[@calculators|calculators]] of this kind are rare, but their skills seem to be built from ordinary brain abilities pushed to an extreme.

Shakuntala Devi wanted other people, especially children, to stop fearing maths. She wrote books such as Figuring: The Joy of Numbers and Puzzles to Puzzle You, full of tricks, riddles and shortcuts. She also wrote on astrology and cookery.

In 1977 she published a book about gay people, one of the first in India to discuss them with sympathy. It was unusual and brave for its time. In 1980 she even [[@election-commission|stood for election]] to the Lok Sabha, India's lower house of [[@parliament-india|Parliament]], though she did not win.

Shakuntala Devi died in Bengaluru on 21 April 2013, aged 83. In 2020, a Hindi film about her life, starring Vidya Balan, brought her story to a new generation. Teachers still use her puzzle books, and her record from 1980 is still talked about whenever people compare human brains with machines.

text: Many ancient peoples counted, but treating zero as a number of its own was a big leap.

Indian mathematicians, especially Brahmagupta, wrote down rules for calculating with zero. In his book of 628 CE, he explained that a number minus itself gives zero, and that anything multiplied by zero is zero.

The digits you use, 0 to 9, are called Hindu-Arabic numerals, because they came from India through the Arab world. No single person invented zero. It grew in India over centuries, and Indian scholars were the first to treat it as a full number.

myth: The Arabs invented the numbers we call Arabic numerals.

The digits 0 to 9 began in India. Scholars in the Arab world, such as al-Khwarizmi, learned them, wrote about them and passed them on. Europeans called them Arabic because that is where they got them.

sec.t:
With zero as a placeholder, ten symbols can write any number: 5, 50, 500. The zero's job is to say "nothing in this place", so the other digits stay in the right columns. [[@roman-numerals|Roman numerals]] had no zero, which made big sums much harder. Try multiplying CCCXLVII by XXIX.

The Babylonians, in today's Iraq, used a mark for an empty place about 2,300 years ago, but never as a number by itself. On the other side of the world, the Maya of Central America invented their own zero for their [[@calendars|calendars]], entirely separately.

sec.h: Carved in stone, written on birch bark
sec.t:
Inside Gwalior Fort, a small temple carries an [[inscription|inscription]] from 876 CE. It lists gifts to the temple, including a garden 270 measures long and 50 garlands of flowers a day. Both numbers end in a clear round 0, one of the oldest dated zeros anyone can still visit.

The Bakhshali [[manuscript|manuscript]] is a maths text written on birch bark, dug up by a farmer near Peshawar in 1881. It uses a dot for zero. In 2017, carbon dating suggested some pages might be very old indeed, but scholars still argue about what the results mean.

Around 825 CE, the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote a book in Baghdad explaining calculation with the [[@indian-numerals|Indian numerals]]. Translated into Latin, it carried his name to Europe, and our word "[[algorithm|algorithm]]" comes from it.

Merchants in North Africa used the new digits for trade. A young Italian named Leonardo of Pisa, later called Fibonacci, learned them there while helping his father, a trade official. In 1202 he published a book showing how much easier they made sums of money, weights and interest. Slowly, over the next few hundred years, Europe gave up its counting boards and Roman numerals.

The [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] word for zero is *shunya*, meaning empty. Arab scholars translated it as *sifr*. In Latin it became *zephirum*, then *zero* in Italian. The same Arabic word gave English "[[cipher|cipher]]", which once meant zero and later came to mean a secret code, as in [[@cipher-codes|secret codes]].

Not everyone welcomed the new numbers. In 1299, the city of Florence banned them in official account books, partly because a 0 could easily be changed into a 6 or a 9. But merchants found the Indian digits far quicker, and they spread along the [[@trade-routes|trade routes]]. Every computer now runs on [[@number-zero-one|zeros and ones]]. text: The Pro Kabaddi League began on 26 July 2014 in Mumbai. A company called Mashal Sports, led by the sports broadcaster Charu Sharma and backed by the businessman Anand Mahindra, wanted to do for [[@kabaddi|kabaddi]] what the [[@ipl|IPL]] had done for cricket. They created city teams, bought TV time, hired commentators and moved the game indoors onto colourful mats.

It worked. Millions of families who had played kabaddi as children, or had never watched it at all, started following teams with names like Bengal Warriors, Telugu Titans and Patna Pirates. Kabaddi became one of the most watched sports on Indian television.

sec.t:
Kabaddi has been played in Indian [[@villages-india|villages]] for a very long time. It needs no ball, bat or net, only a patch of flat ground and two teams. A raider crosses into the other half, tries to tag defenders and gets back, all while chanting "kabaddi, kabaddi" so everyone can hear they haven't taken a breath. The defenders try to stop the raider from returning.

India dominated kabaddi at the Asian Games for decades, winning every men's gold from 1990 until 2018, when Iran won. India took the title back in 2023. But kabaddi had rarely been on TV, and top players often struggled to earn a living from the sport. Many worked for the railways, the police, the army or banks, which hired sportspeople and gave them time to train.

The league turned players into stars. Pardeep Narwal, nicknamed the "Dubki King" for ducking under linked arms, became the league's top raider. Defenders like Fazel Atrachali from Iran became famous for crushing tackles. Players from Iran, South Korea, Bangladesh and Kenya have all played in the league.

Raiders need fast feet and quick decisions. Defenders need strong grip, balance and powerful [[@muscles|muscles]] in the legs and back. Teams now have fitness trainers, video analysts and physiotherapists, just as football and cricket clubs do.

The first season, in 2014, had eight teams. Jaipur Pink Panthers won the trophy. The league grew to twelve teams in 2017, and Patna Pirates won three titles in a row in 2016 and 2017. In 2025, Season 12 ended with Dabang Delhi beating Puneri Paltan 31 to 28 in a close final, for their second title.

The success of Pro Kabaddi encouraged other traditional sports. Ultimate Kho Kho, a professional league for [[@kho-kho|kho-kho]], started in 2022. Kabaddi itself has spread too. It is played at the [[@asian-games|Asian Games]], and countries from Iran to Kenya now send players to India to learn and compete.

For many village players, the league opened a door that didn't exist before. A good raider from a small town in Haryana or Tamil Nadu can now earn a professional salary, play in big indoor arenas and see his face on posters across the country.

text: A cricket ball starts with a small ball of cork at its centre. Layers of cork and tightly wound string are built up around it until it's hard and the right size. That core is covered in leather, dyed red, white or pink, and stitched together along a raised seam.

A football is built the other way round: it's hollow. Inside is a rubber bladder, which holds the air. Around it go layers of cloth for strength, then an outer skin of synthetic leather made of panels. Some balls are stitched by hand, some by machine and many top balls are now glued and heat-bonded with no stitches at all.

Both have to meet strict rules on size and weight, so that a ball in Chennai behaves like one in Manchester. A full-size football for top matches must measure 68 to 70 cm around and weigh 410 to 450 grams.

sec.t:
The Laws of Cricket say a men's ball must weigh between 155.9 and 163 grams. The best balls have a leather cover cut into four pieces, sewn into two halves and then joined around the middle with the main seam. Six rows of stitches make that seam stand out.

In the top balls, the seam is stitched by hand with waxed thread. The ball is then pressed in a mould, polished and stamped with gold lettering.

Three makers dominate Test cricket. Kookaburra, from Australia, is used in most countries. Dukes, made in England, has a very prominent seam that helps bowlers [[@cricket-swing|swing]] the ball. SG, from Meerut in Uttar Pradesh, is used for Test matches in India.

Red balls are traditional for Test matches. White balls are used in one-day and T20 games, because they're easier to see under floodlights against dark backgrounds. White balls tend to wear and get dirty faster, so players in one-dayers use one from each end.

The pink ball was created for day-night Test matches. The first was played in Adelaide, Australia, in 2015. Its colour shows up well both in late sunlight and under lights.

Since the 2000s, top footballs have used fewer, curved panels glued together with heat instead of stitches. That makes them rounder and more waterproof. But fewer seams can also change how a ball moves through the air. Some players complained that smooth balls wobbled unpredictably.

The ball for the 2026 World Cup, played in the USA, Canada and Mexico, is called Trionda. It has just four panels, deep grooves to steady its flight, and a small motion [[sensor|sensor]] inside that sends data to the video referees.

American footballs are pointed at both ends, which makes them easier to throw in a spiral. They are made of four leather panels with a row of laces for grip. They're still often called "pigskins", even though the leather is cowhide.

A good grip matters in every sport. Leather cricket balls, laces on American footballs and dimpled panels on soccer balls all rely on [[@friction|friction]] to let players control where the ball goes.

text: Your mouth is home to hundreds of kinds of [[bacteria|bacteria]]. Most are harmless, but a few, such as one called Streptococcus mutans, love sugar. When you eat sweets, biscuits or even white bread, these bacteria feast on the sugars and give off [[acid|acid]] as waste.

That acid slowly [[dissolve|dissolves]] the hard outer coat of your teeth, called [[enamel|enamel]]. One attack does little harm, and your [[saliva|saliva]] helps repair it. But if sugar keeps arriving all day, the acid wins, and a weak spot becomes a hole. That hole is a cavity, also called tooth decay or dental caries.
