sec.h: The sticky film on your teeth
sec.t:
If you run your tongue over your teeth before brushing in the morning, they may feel fuzzy. That's [[plaque|plaque]], a sticky film of bacteria. It clings to teeth, especially in the grooves of back teeth, between teeth and along the gums.

Bacteria in plaque are protected from your saliva, so the acid they make stays pressed against the enamel. Brushing twice a day breaks up the film. Cleaning between teeth with floss or a small brush reaches places a [[@toothbrush|toothbrush]] misses. If plaque is left for days, it hardens into tartar, which only a dentist can remove.

sec.h: It's how often, not just how much
sec.t:
The surprising part is that how often you eat sugar matters more than how much. After each sugary snack or drink, the mouth turns acidic for roughly half an hour. Then saliva washes the acid away and helps rebuild the enamel.

So a child who has one sweet with lunch gives their teeth one short attack. A child who sips juice or a fizzy drink all afternoon, or nibbles biscuits every hour, keeps the acid going for hours. Sticky foods like toffees and dried fruit cling to teeth and stretch out the attack too. [[@sugar|Sugar]] hides in many foods, including ketchup, flavoured yoghurt and some breakfast cereals.

Fluoride is a mineral that makes enamel tougher and helps it repair itself. In the 1930s and 1940s, American scientists noticed that people in towns with natural fluoride in their water had fewer cavities. In 1945, Grand Rapids in Michigan became the first city to add a small amount of fluoride to its tap water on purpose.

Today most toothpastes contain fluoride. Dentists advise using a small amount, about the size of a pea for children, and spitting it out without rinsing too much afterwards, so a little stays on the teeth.

sec.h: The tooth worm and other old ideas
sec.t:
For thousands of years, many people believed toothache came from worms boring into teeth. The idea appears in old Babylonian writings and in folk beliefs from India, China and Europe. In the 1700s, the French dentist Pierre Fauchard argued against it. Like many old ideas that [[@doctors-history|doctors]] later dropped, it gave way to the real cause: bacteria and acid.

Tooth decay is still very common. The World Health Organization estimated in 2022 that about 2 billion people have decay in their adult teeth. Yet it is also one of the most preventable diseases. Brushing with fluoride toothpaste, cutting down on sugary snacks between meals, and seeing a dentist regularly keep most cavities away.

text: Alan Turing was a British mathematician who helped invent the idea of the modern computer. In 1936 he described a simple imaginary machine, now called a Turing machine, that could carry out any step-by-step calculation. Every computer, phone and smartwatch works on that principle.

During the Second World War he was a leading codebreaker at Bletchley Park, helping read secret German messages. He later asked whether machines could think, a question at the heart of [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]]. His life ended sadly and early, but his reputation has grown and grown.

st.prompt: In 1950 Turing suggested a test for whether a machine can think. What did it involve?

options.t: Whether a person chatting by text could tell the machine from a human
Whether the machine could beat a person at chess
Whether the machine could solve harder sums than a person

st.reveal: Turing called it the imitation game. A judge types questions to a hidden human and a hidden machine. If the judge cannot reliably tell which is which, Turing said, we should take seriously the idea that the machine is thinking. People still argue about whether this is a good test.

n.certNote: Turing's ideas and his codebreaking work are well documented. How much Bletchley Park shortened the Second World War is debated, and some historians question the official ruling on how he died.

d.try: Make a code wheel. Write the alphabet around the edge of two paper circles, one slightly smaller, and lay the small one on top. Turn it three letters along and use it to write a secret message, A becoming D, B becoming E. Swap with a friend and break each other's codes. Enigma worked on a similar idea, but its wheels moved with every letter.
myth: Alan Turing broke the Enigma code on his own and invented the computer.

Polish mathematicians first broke Enigma in the 1930s and shared their methods with Britain. Turing led much of the work on German naval codes, but Bletchley Park had thousands of staff. The first large electronic codebreaking computer there, Colossus, was built by engineer Tommy Flowers for a different code.

sec.h: A boy who did his own experiments
sec.t:
Turing was born in London in 1912. His parents worked in India, where his father was in the Indian Civil Service, so Alan and his brother were mostly raised by a family in England. He was untidy, shy and always experimenting. At boarding school, teachers complained he cared more about science than anything else.

He was also a very fast runner. While at Bletchley Park, he sometimes ran up to about 64 kilometres to London for meetings. In 1947 he ran a [[@running-marathon|marathon]] in 2 hours 46 minutes, close to the time needed for the British Olympic team.

In 1939, as the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] began, Turing joined Britain's secret codebreaking centre at Bletchley Park, north of London. The German forces used a machine called Enigma to scramble their radio messages. Its settings changed every day, giving millions upon millions of possible combinations.

Polish mathematicians had already cracked earlier versions and built a machine to help. Building on their work, Turing designed a much faster machine called the Bombe, which tested possible settings at high speed. He also led work on the hardest code of all, used by [[@submarines|German submarines]] in the Atlantic. Reading those messages helped ships carrying food and supplies avoid attack.

After the war, Turing designed one of the first stored-program computers and then worked on early computers in Manchester. In 1950 he wrote a paper asking "Can machines think?" and proposed the imitation game, now known as the Turing test.

In 1952 he turned to biology. He suggested how simple chemicals spreading and reacting in a growing animal could make spots and stripes. Scientists have since found his ideas at work in the patterns of fish, shells and perhaps even [[@tiger-stripes|tiger stripes]].

In 1952 Turing was convicted under British laws of the time that made relationships between men a crime. He lost his security clearance and was forced to undergo [[hormone|hormone]] treatment. He died in 1954, aged 41. An inquest said he had taken his own life, though some historians have questioned this.

Britain later changed those laws. In 2009 the Prime Minister made a public apology, and in 2013 Turing received a royal pardon. Since 2021, his face has appeared on the Bank of England's £50 note. The top prize in computer science, the Turing Award, has carried his name since 1966.

text: Surgical robots are tools that let [[surgeon|surgeons]] operate through a few small holes instead of a large cut. The surgeon sits at a console a few metres from the patient, looks into a 3D viewer and moves hand controls. Robotic arms beside the operating table copy those movements with thin instruments and a tiny camera inside the body.

The robot doesn't decide anything. What it adds is precision. It can shrink a big hand movement into a tiny one, filter out shaking, and bend its "wrists" in ways human hands can't inside a small space. The best-known system, da Vinci, was approved in the United States in 2000 and is now used in many countries, including India.

options.t: The surgeon, who controls every movement from a console
The robot, using its own artificial intelligence
A computer program written before the operation

st.reveal: Systems like da Vinci don't move on their own. The surgeon sits at a console, looks through a 3D viewer and moves hand controls. The robot copies those movements with tiny instruments inside the patient.

d.try: Hold a pencil at arm's length and try to keep its tip perfectly still against a dot on paper for 30 seconds. Notice the small wobble. Now rest your wrist on the table and try again. Surgical robots remove that wobble electronically, which is one reason surgeons use them.
myth: In robotic surgery, a robot operates on you by itself.

Today's surgical robots are tools, not doctors. A trained surgeon controls every movement, and other doctors and nurses stand beside the patient throughout. Fully self-operating surgery robots are still being researched.

sec.t:
Before robots, surgeons were already doing keyhole surgery. They pushed long, thin tools and a camera through small cuts and watched a screen. Patients healed faster, with less pain and smaller scars. But it was awkward. The tools were stiff, the picture was flat, and moving a hand left made the tool's tip go right, like using chopsticks through a letterbox.

A robot fixes much of this. Its instruments have [[@joints|joints]] near the tip that can turn and twist. The camera gives a magnified 3D view, a bit like looking through powerful [[@lenses-glasses|lenses]]. And the controls move the natural way.

Everyone's hands shake very slightly, even a top surgeon's. A robot's computer can filter that out. It can also scale movements, so moving a hand 3 cm moves the instrument just 1 cm. This helps with delicate work like stitching tiny blood vessels or removing a tumour close to a nerve.

Robots are often used for operations on the prostate, the [[@kidneys|kidneys]], the womb and the heart, where the space is small and the work is fiddly. Many big hospitals in Indian cities now have surgical robots, and some Indian companies have started making their own.

On 7 September 2001, a team led by the French surgeon Jacques Marescaux sat in New York and removed the gall bladder of a 68-year-old woman in Strasbourg, France. A robot in Strasbourg copied their movements, sent over a high-speed fibre-optic link. Surgeons stood by in France in case anything went wrong. It was called Operation Lindbergh, after the pilot who first flew alone across the Atlantic.

The hardest part was the delay. If the video arrives late, the surgeon's hands get ahead of what they can see. Fast networks such as [[@5g|5G]] and fibre may make [[@future-medicine|long-distance surgery]] more common, especially for places without specialists.

Surgeons train for many hours on simulators before using a robot on patients, a bit like pilots in a flight simulator. Researchers are now testing robots that can do small tasks by themselves, such as stitching, under a surgeon's eye. For now, the [[@robots|robot]] is like a very steady, very precise pair of hands that always waits for instructions.

text: The Emergency was a period of 21 months, from 25 June 1975 to 21 March 1977, when the government of Prime Minister [[@indira-gandhi|Indira Gandhi]] used special powers in the [[@constitution|Constitution]]. President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed declared a national emergency on her advice, citing a threat of "internal disturbance".

During this time, many fundamental rights were suspended. Newspapers had to show stories to censors before printing. More than 100,000 people, including opposition leaders and activists, were detained without trial, and elections due in 1976 were postponed. In 1977 the government called elections, lost heavily, and the Emergency ended.

st.prompt: In 1976, India's Supreme Court decided whether people jailed during the Emergency could challenge their detention in court. What did most of the judges decide?

options.t: That they could not, while the Emergency lasted
That all detainees must be freed at once
That the Emergency itself was illegal

st.reveal: Four of the five judges ruled that the right to go to court against detention was suspended during the Emergency. Justice H.R. Khanna disagreed. In 2017 the Supreme Court said the majority had been wrong.

n.certNote: The facts of what the government did are well documented, including by an official inquiry. People still disagree about how to judge the period. The government of the time said it was needed to restore order, while critics see it as a serious attack on democracy.

myth: The Emergency was a military takeover.

The army played no political role. The Emergency was declared by the President on the advice of the elected government, using powers in the Constitution. That is one reason the rules were later changed to make such powers harder to use.

sec.t:
In the early 1970s, India faced high prices, shortages and strikes. In Gujarat and Bihar, students led big protests. The veteran leader Jayaprakash Narayan, known as JP, called for "total revolution" against corruption and the government.

Then, on 12 June 1975, the Allahabad High Court found that Indira Gandhi had broken election rules in her 1971 campaign. It cancelled her election to [[@parliament-india|Parliament]]. She appealed to the Supreme Court. Opposition parties demanded she resign, and JP called for a nationwide protest campaign, urging police and soldiers not to obey orders they believed were illegal. On the night of 25 June, the Emergency was declared.

In 1976, the [[@supreme-courts|Supreme Court]] heard a case about whether detainees could challenge their arrest in court, a right known as habeas corpus. Four of the five judges ruled that they could not while the Emergency lasted. Justice H.R. Khanna wrote a lone disagreement, arguing that the right to life could not simply be switched off. He was later passed over for Chief Justice.

[[parliament|Parliament]] also passed the 42nd Amendment, one of the biggest changes ever made to the Constitution. It reduced the powers of courts, among other things, and added the words "socialist" and "secular" to the Preamble.

The Emergency also brought campaigns that hurt many poor families. In some areas, officials, under pressure to meet targets, forced men to undergo sterilisation operations as part of a population control drive. [[@slums-housing|Slums]] were demolished in Delhi, most notoriously near Turkman Gate. These drives were closely linked to the Prime Minister's son, Sanjay Gandhi.

Supporters of the Emergency pointed to other changes, such as fewer strikes and trains running more on time. The later Shah Commission, set up to investigate, found many cases of abuse of power.

In January 1977, Indira Gandhi announced elections and released many prisoners. Opposition parties joined together as the Janata Party. In March, voters threw out the government. Indira Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi both lost their seats, and Morarji Desai became Prime Minister.

The new government passed the 44th Amendment in 1978. It replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion", and said the cabinet must advise the President in writing before an emergency could be declared. Indira Gandhi herself returned to power in the 1980 election. For many Indians, the lesson of the Emergency was that the [[@vote-how|vote]] could still change a government.

text: The Mughals were a [[dynasty|dynasty]] of emperors who ruled much of the Indian [[subcontinent|subcontinent]] from 1526 until the 1700s, and in name until 1857. They were Muslims, descended from the Central Asian conquerors Timur and [[@genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]].

At its biggest, around 1700, their [[empire|empire]] covered almost all of today's India, Pakistan and [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]], and part of Afghanistan. It was one of the richest and most populous states in the world. The Mughals built the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]] and the Red Fort, supported painters, poets and musicians, and left a mark on everything from Indian food to the [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] and Urdu languages. After about 1720, their power faded, and the British took over.

st.prompt: How did Babur win the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 against a much bigger army?

options.t: He used cannons and guns, and tied carts together as a barrier
He bribed the enemy's elephants with sugarcane
He attacked at night while everyone slept

st.reveal: Babur had only about 12,000 to 25,000 men by most estimates. He linked carts into a wall, fired cannons and matchlock guns from behind it, and sent horse archers round the sides. Gunpowder weapons were still rare in India, and the noise panicked Ibrahim Lodi's war elephants.

myth: The Mughals were foreigners who never became Indian.
Babur came from Central Asia, but his descendants were born and buried in India, married into Indian families, spoke Hindustani and shaped Indian food, music, art and language for centuries.

sec.t:
Babur was born in 1483 in Fergana, a valley in today's Uzbekistan. He became a king at 11, lost his kingdom, won Samarkand and lost it again. Eventually he settled in Kabul.

From there he raided India. In 1526, at Panipat near Delhi, his small army defeated the last [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultan]], Ibrahim Lodi, using cannons and guns. Babur wrote an unusually honest diary called the *Baburnama* in his own Turkic language. He describes battles, gardens, animals and his longing for the fruits of home.

Humayun's son [[@akbar|Akbar]] ruled for nearly 50 years and made the empire strong. He worked with [[@rajputs|Rajput]] kings and tried to bring people of different faiths together.

Jahangir, his son, loved nature and art and had painters record birds, flowers and animals in fine detail. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and a new walled city in Delhi with the Red Fort. Aurangzeb ruled for 49 years and pushed the empire to its largest size. He was a strict Muslim ruler. Historians still argue about his policies, including the return of the jizya tax on non-Muslims and the wars he fought for decades in the Deccan.

The Mughals loved gardens divided into four parts by water channels, called *charbagh*. You can see them at Humayun's Tomb, the Taj Mahal and the Shalimar Bagh in Srinagar.

Court painters made tiny, detailed [[@mughal-miniatures|miniature paintings]]. Persian, Central Asian and Indian cooking blended into rich dishes such as kormas and kebabs. Many words in Hindi and Urdu came from the Persian spoken at court.

After Aurangzeb died in 1707, the empire weakened. Provinces broke away, the [[@marathas|Marathas]] grew powerful, and in 1739 the Persian ruler Nader Shah sacked Delhi and carried off the jewel-covered [[@peacock-tail|Peacock Throne]].

The [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] gradually took control. By 1857, the emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, a poet, ruled little beyond the Red Fort. After the revolt that year, the British sent him into exile in Rangoon, where he died in 1862. The dynasty ended there, far from Fergana and far from Delhi.

text: During and after the Second World War, an American aircraft lab called Langley, in Hampton, Virginia, hired hundreds of women to do maths. They worked out how air flowed over wings, how planes behaved and later how rockets should fly. Their job title was "computer".

Some of them were Black women. Because Virginia's laws kept Black and white people apart, they worked in a separate office, the West Area Computing unit, and had to use separate dining tables and toilets. Despite that, their work helped send Americans into [[orbit|orbit]] and to the Moon.
The 2016 book and film Hidden Figures told the story of three of them: Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson.

d.try: Time yourself adding up a column of ten three-digit numbers by hand, then check your answer with a calculator. Try a second column and see if you get faster. Langley's human computers did thousands of steps like this, and their answers had to be exactly right.
myth: The early space programme was the work of a few famous astronauts and engineers.

Thousands of people made it work, including hundreds of women "computers". Some of them, like Katherine Johnson, did calculations that astronauts' lives depended on, but their names were almost unknown for decades.

sec.t:
In the 1940s, there were no laptops and few electronic computers. Engineers testing a new plane in a wind tunnel came back with pages of measurements. Turning them into useful answers took huge amounts of arithmetic.

The human computers did it with pencils, paper, slide rules and noisy desk calculating machines. One problem could take days. A single mistake could mean a plane design that did not fly, so the work had to be exact. Many of these women had trained as maths teachers, because few other jobs were open to them.

Mary Jackson started as a computer in 1951. She was invited to work in a wind tunnel team, and her boss encouraged her to train as an engineer. To do that, she needed courses held at a whites-only high school. She asked the City of Hampton for special permission to attend, and got it.

In 1958, she became NASA's first Black female engineer. Later in her career, she worked to help other women and minorities get hired and promoted. In 2020, NASA renamed its headquarters building in Washington, DC, after her.

Katherine Johnson was so good at maths that she started high school at age 10. At Langley she worked on flight paths, calculating exactly where a spacecraft would go and land.

In 1962, the astronaut John Glenn was about to become the first American to orbit Earth. NASA had begun using new electronic computers to plan the flight. Glenn did not fully trust them. He asked for Johnson to check the numbers by hand. She did, matching the machine's results, and Glenn flew.

She later worked on calculations for the [[@moon-race-women|Apollo 11]] Moon landing. In 2015, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and she lived to 101.

For decades, these women were barely mentioned in histories of the [[@space-race|space race]]. That changed when Margot Lee Shetterly, whose father worked at Langley, wrote Hidden Figures. In 2019, the street outside NASA headquarters was renamed Hidden Figures Way.

There are similar stories in India. When ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars in 2014, photos of women scientists celebrating in saris went round the world. Women have since led major Indian missions, including as project director of Chandrayaan-2. And the machines that replaced the human computers began as giant rooms full of glowing valves, as you can see in the story of the [[@first-computers|first computers]].

text: India produces more milk than any other country, roughly a quarter of the world's total. It wasn't always so. In the 1950s and 1960s, Indian cities often faced milk shortages, and the country imported milk powder.

The change is called the White Revolution. It grew from a farmers' cooperative in Anand, Gujarat, which became the famous brand [[@amul|Amul]]. A young engineer, Verghese Kurien, helped build it. From 1970, a national programme called Operation Flood copied the Anand model across India, linking villages to cities. In 1998, India overtook the USA as the world's largest milk producer.

Farmers had to switch to cows

st.reveal: Amul's dairy expert H.M. Dalaya, working with Kurien, developed a method to make powder and baby food from buffalo milk. It meant Indian farmers' surplus milk in winter could be stored and sold all year.

Most of India's milk comes from millions of small farmers, many with only a few cows or buffaloes. Village cooperatives collect it twice a day and send it to big dairies for processing.

sec.t:
In the 1940s, dairy farmers around Kaira district in Gujarat sold their milk to a private dairy that supplied Bombay. The farmers felt they were paid too little. Their leaders went to [[@sardar-patel|Sardar Patel]], who advised them to form their own cooperative.

A cooperative is a business owned by its members, who share the profits. In 1946, after a milk strike, the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union was registered in Anand. Local leader Tribhuvandas Patel led it. It was later named Amul, from a [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] word, *amulya*, meaning priceless.

Since 1966, Amul has been advertised by a cartoon girl in a polka-dot dress. Her billboards make jokes about the news of the week, and they have run for so long that grandparents and grandchildren both know her.

Verghese Kurien was born in [[@kerala|Kerala]] in 1921 and trained as an engineer. In 1949 the government sent him to Anand to work at a small creamery. He planned to leave as soon as he could.

Instead he stayed for decades. He fixed the cooperative's machines, then helped grow it into one of India's biggest food businesses. Each village had its own society, where farmers brought milk twice a day. Their milk was tested for fat and they were paid according to quality, often on the spot.

sec.h: A film paid for by farmers
sec.t: In 1976, director Shyam Benegal made a film, *Manthan*, about a dairy cooperative. About five lakh Gujarat farmers each gave ₹2 to fund it, making them its producers. When it was released, farmers came by the truckload to watch "their" film. A restored version was shown at the Cannes Film Festival in 2024.

sec.h: Why it worked, and what's next
sec.t:
The cooperative model let small farmers, including many women and landless families, earn a steady income from just a couple of animals. Payment came regularly, which helped families plan.

There are challenges. Many Indian cows and buffaloes give less milk than those on big Western farms, and feeding and caring for animals in heat waves is getting harder. Some people also raise questions about animal welfare and the environment.

Still, think of a glass of [[@milk|milk]], a bowl of curd or a block of [[@cheese-paneer|paneer]] in an Indian home. It very likely started with a small farmer carrying a steel can to the village society.

text: The Dead Sea is a salt lake in the Middle East, with Jordan on its eastern shore and Israel and the West Bank on its western shore. Its water is so salty that about a third of its weight is [[dissolve|dissolved]] salts. That makes it much heavier, or denser, than ordinary water.

Your body is about as dense as fresh water, so in a pool you just barely float. In the Dead Sea, the water is around a quarter heavier than you are. It pushes you up so strongly that you bob on top like a cork, with your feet and shoulders out of the water. Trying to swim face down is hard, and splashing is a bad idea, because the water stings your eyes badly.

st.prompt: Why does your body float so easily in the Dead Sea?

options.t: The salty water is much denser than your body
Gas bubbles from the seabed push you up
Salt soaks into your skin and makes you lighter

st.reveal: A litre of Dead Sea water weighs about 1.24 kg, while a litre of fresh water weighs 1 kg. Your body is about as dense as fresh water. In water this heavy, it only needs to sink a little way to push aside its own weight, so most of you stays above the surface.

sec.t:
The Dead Sea lies at the bottom of a long, deep valley formed where two pieces of the Earth's crust are sliding past each other. The water's surface is about 440 m below sea level (2025), lower than any other dry land on Earth.

Water flows in, mostly from the Jordan River, but it has nowhere to go. No river flows out. In the hot, dry desert, water evaporates fast and leaves its salts behind. Over thousands of years, those salts have built up to roughly ten times the saltiness of the ocean. It is among the saltiest [[@lakes-salty|lakes]] on Earth, although a few, such as Lake Assal in Djibouti and Don Juan Pond in Antarctica, are even saltier.

Since the 1960s, the Dead Sea has fallen by more than 30 m. In recent decades it has dropped by about a metre a year. Most of the Jordan River's water is now taken for farms and cities before it reaches the lake. Factories also pump Dead Sea water into shallow ponds to collect minerals like potash, which is used in [[fertiliser|fertiliser]].

As the water retreats, fresh groundwater dissolves buried layers of salt under the old shore. The ground above collapses into [[@sinkholes|sinkholes]]. Thousands have formed, swallowing parts of roads, beaches and farms. Hotels once built on the beach now sit a long walk from the water.

The land around the Dead Sea, less than an hour's drive from [[@jerusalem|Jerusalem]], has long attracted people. In 1947, a young shepherd exploring caves at Qumran, near the northern shore, found clay jars holding ancient scrolls. The Dead Sea Scrolls, about 2,000 years old, include some of the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible.

On the southern shore, salt forms crusts, pillars and white rings around rocks. India has salt landscapes too. In the [[@gujarat-rann|Rann of Kutch]] in Gujarat, a seasonal shallow sea dries into a vast white salt desert every winter. Neither place is a sea you can swim in for long, but only one lets you float like a beach ball.

text: Delhi is very old, but nobody can give one exact birthday. In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas built a city called Indraprastha on the Yamuna, and many people believe it stood where Delhi is now. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] digging at Purana Qila have found pottery and remains over 2,500 years old. An [[inscription|inscription]] of Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], carved on a rock more than 2,200 years ago, was also found in south Delhi in 1966.

What we know for certain is that Delhi has been a capital again and again for about a thousand years. Each ruler built a new city beside the old one, so modern Delhi is really many cities stitched together.

st.prompt: Delhi's famous Iron Pillar has stood outdoors in rain and sun. For about how long?

About 200 years

st.reveal: The pillar was made in the time of the Gupta kings, about 1,600 years ago. It was later moved to the Qutb complex. It has hardly rusted because its iron contains phosphorus, which helps a thin protective layer form on the surface.

myth: Delhi's Iron Pillar has never rusted at all.
It has rusted a little, but very slowly. Scientists found that a thin, tight layer of iron compounds formed on the surface, helped by phosphorus in the metal, and it protects the iron underneath.

sec.t:
Historians often speak of "seven cities of Delhi", though they do not all agree on the list. One version starts with Lal Kot and Qila Rai Pithora, the fort of the Tomar and Chauhan kings. Then come Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah and Firozabad, built by the rulers of the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]. Sher Shah Suri and Humayun built around Purana Qila. Shah Jahan built the seventh, Shahjahanabad, which we now call Old Delhi.

Ruins of all of them still stand. You can walk from a 14th-century wall to a Metro station in ten minutes.

sec.h: Stone towers and an iron pillar

sec.t: In 1639, the [[@mughals|Mughal]] emperor Shah Jahan, who also built the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]], began a new capital. Its heart was the Red Fort, finished in 1648, with marble halls and canals of water running through them. Chandni Chowk, the main street in front, became one of India's great markets and still is. Every Independence Day, the Prime Minister raises the national flag at the Red Fort.

Some of Delhi's most beautiful buildings are tombs. Humayun's Tomb, finished in the 1570s, sits in a square garden divided by water channels into four parts. This kind of garden, called a charbagh, came to India from Persia and Central Asia. Many historians see the tomb as an early model for the Taj Mahal, built about 80 years later. Close by lies the shrine of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya, where singers still perform [[@qawwali|qawwali]] music on Thursday evenings, as they have for centuries.

In 1911, the British announced they would move the capital of India from Calcutta to Delhi. Architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker planned a new city with wide avenues, gardens and grand buildings in stone. New Delhi was opened in 1931. After independence in 1947, it became the capital of free India, and the [[@parliament-india|Parliament]] meets there.

Delhi now spreads far beyond its old walls. Its wider urban area holds well over 3 crore people, one of the biggest in the world. The city has a large Metro, first opened in 2002, and also struggles with traffic and [[@air-pollution|air pollution]], especially in winter. Yet a farmer from the Mughal age would still recognise the river, the Red Fort and the call of [[@people-street-vendors|street sellers]] in Chandni Chowk.

text: Thousands of years ago, a rock from space came screaming through the sky over what is now Maharashtra. It was travelling at perhaps 20 km every second, fast enough to cross Mumbai in under two seconds. When it hit the ground, it blasted out a bowl about 1.8 km wide and about 150 m deep.

Over time, rain and underground springs filled the bottom of the bowl with water. Today that water is Lonar Lake, ringed by forest, old temples and steep [[crater|crater]] walls. It's one of the best-preserved young [[@meteorites|meteorite]] craters on Earth.

st.prompt: Why did scientists get so excited that Lonar crater is made of basalt rock?

options.t: Basalt craters look like craters on the Moon and Mars, so Lonar helps us study them
Basalt is the only rock a meteor can break
Basalt contains gold from space

st.reveal: Much of the Moon's and Mars's surface is basalt, an old lava rock. Lonar is one of very few young, clear impact craters on Earth made in basalt, so it is a natural laboratory for space scientists.

src: Geological Survey of India, Lonar Crater National Geological Monument.
Jourdan F. et al. (2011) 40Ar/39Ar age of the Lonar crater and consequence for the geochronology of planetary impacts, Geology.
Ramsar Convention Secretariat, Lonar Lake site information.
n.certNote: Scientists agree Lonar is an impact crater, but its age is debated. Older studies said about 50,000 years; a 2011 study suggested about 5,70,000 years.

myth: Lonar Lake was made by a volcano, like most round lakes.
For a long time some people thought so, because the Deccan is old volcanic land. But Lonar has shocked minerals and glassy bits of melted rock that only a high-speed impact can make.

sec.h: A punch harder than a bomb
sec.t:
The space rock was probably only a few dozen metres across, smaller than a cricket ground. Size isn't the scary part. Speed is. At those speeds, the rock carried more energy than a large bomb, and much of it turned into heat and pressure in a split second.

The rock vaporised. Ground rock was squeezed so hard that its crystals were changed in ways ordinary forces can't manage. Some of it melted into small glassy beads. Finding these "shocked" minerals in the 1970s helped prove that Lonar was not a volcano at all.

The blast also flung rock outwards in every direction. Look at the crater today and you can still see a raised rim about 20 to 30 m high. It is made of rock layers that were peeled back and flipped over like the pages of a book. Smaller pieces landed far beyond the rim as a blanket of broken stone.

{{story:asteroid-size}}

Lonar sits on the [[@deccan|Deccan Traps]], layers of [[basalt|basalt]] from enormous [[lava|lava]] flows about 66 million years ago. That is the same time a much bigger space rock struck Mexico and the dinosaurs died out, which makes scientists argue about [[@dino-extinction-theories|what really killed them]].

Basalt matters because the Moon and Mars are covered in it. Lonar lets scientists walk around a basalt impact crater on Earth and compare it with ones seen by spacecraft. Researchers from NASA, ISRO and Indian universities have all studied it.

How old is Lonar? Here, scientists disagree. Earlier estimates said about 50,000 years. A 2011 study using argon dating suggested about 5,70,000 years. New dating methods may settle it.

sec.h: The day the lake turned pink
sec.t:
Lonar's water is very salty and very alkaline, like water with lots of soap [[dissolve|dissolved]] in it. Few fish can live in it, but tiny [[microbe|microbes]] thrive.

In June 2020, people living nearby noticed something odd. Within a few days, the green lake had turned pink. Scientists tested the water and found huge numbers of salt-loving microbes called haloarchaea, which make a pink [[pigment|pigment]]. A hot summer had evaporated water and made the lake even saltier, giving them a boom. The same thing tints [[@earth-weird-pink-lakes|pink lakes]] in Australia and Senegal.

People have lived around Lonar for a very long time. Ruined temples stand on the slopes, and the Daitya Sudan temple in the town is about 800 years old. A local story says the crater was where the god Vishnu defeated a demon named Lonasur, who hid underground.

In 1823, a British officer named C. J. E. Alexander described the crater in writing, which is often counted as its first scientific mention. Today Lonar is a Ramsar [[wetland|wetland]] and a national geological monument. Peafowl call from the forest on its rim, and many kinds of birds feed along the shore, as they do in other [[@wetlands|wetlands]] across India.

text: Morocco is a country in the north-west corner of Africa, facing both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. At its northern tip it is only about 14 kilometres from Spain, across the Strait of Gibraltar. It is a kingdom, ruled by a king together with an elected [[parliament|parliament]].

Inside its borders you can find almost every kind of landscape. The Atlas Mountains run through the middle, with snow on their peaks in winter. To the south and east, they drop down to rocky plains and the dunes of the [[@sahara|Sahara]]. Along the coasts are busy ports and beaches. Morocco's old walled cities, called medinas, are mazes of narrow lanes, markets and workshops.

myth: Marrakesh or Casablanca is the capital of Morocco.

sec.t:
The first known people of North Africa were the Amazigh, often called Berbers. Many Moroccans are Amazigh, and in 2011 their language, Tamazight, became an official language alongside [[@arabic-script|Arabic]]. It has its own alphabet, Tifinagh, which you can see on road signs.

Arab armies brought Islam to the region in the 7th century. Later, Moroccan [[dynasty|dynasties]] ruled parts of Spain, and Jews and Muslims expelled from Spain after 1492 settled in Moroccan cities. France and Spain controlled most of Morocco in the early 1900s, and it became independent in 1956. That is why many people speak French as well as Arabic, and why Moroccan food, music and buildings mix so many traditions.

In 1304, a boy named [[@ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] was born in Tangier, on Morocco's northern coast. At 21 he set off for [[@mecca-hajj|Mecca]] and kept going for nearly 30 years. He travelled through the Middle East, Central Asia and India, where he worked as a judge in Delhi, then on to China. On returning home he dictated the story of his travels, one of the great travel books of history.

Moroccan builders cover walls and fountains with zellige, [[mosaic|mosaics]] of small hand-cut clay tiles. The pieces are cut into stars, crosses and polygons, then fitted together into patterns with no gaps, a beautiful kind of [[@tessellations|tessellation]]. Many patterns are built around eight-pointed and twelve-pointed stars.

Guests are welcomed with sweet green mint [[@tea|tea]], poured from high above the glass to make it froth. Families cook in a tagine, a clay pot with a tall cone-shaped lid that sends steam back down onto the food. Couscous, tiny steamed balls of wheat, is a Friday favourite.

In the south-west, argan trees grow in dry, rocky land, almost nowhere else on Earth. Goats climb into them to eat the leaves and fruit, and local women crack the hard nuts to press argan oil.

text: Neuschwanstein is a white castle with pointed towers, perched on a rocky ridge in the Bavarian Alps of southern Germany. It is often called the fairy-tale castle, and it helped inspire Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland in California, which opened in 1955.

It was built for King Ludwig II of Bavaria, starting in 1869. Though it looks [[medieval|medieval]], it is younger than the Taj Mahal by more than 200 years. It went up at about the same time as Mumbai's great Victorian railway terminus, now Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus. Ludwig didn't want a castle for war. He wanted a dream made real.

st.reveal: Work began in 1869 and was still going when King Ludwig II died in 1886. It had modern comforts for its time, including warm-air heating and a telephone.

myth: Neuschwanstein was built to defend Bavaria from enemies.
It was never a fortress. By the 1860s, castles were useless against cannons. Ludwig built it as a private retreat and a stage set for his love of legends and opera.

sec.t:
Ludwig became king of Bavaria in 1864, when he was 18. Bavaria then was a kingdom in its own right. Two years later it lost a war against Prussia, and in 1871 it became part of the new German Empire. Ludwig still wore a crown, but real power had slipped away.

He turned instead to art, music and building. He adored the operas of Richard Wagner, which were full of knights, swans and old German legends. Ludwig paid many of Wagner's debts and helped fund his theatre. Neuschwanstein, which means "New Swan Stone", was to be a castle out of those [[@opera|operas]].

sec.h: Old on the outside, new on the inside

sec.t:
Building went slowly and cost far more than planned. Ludwig paid with his own money, not the state's, but he borrowed heavily. By 1886 his debts were enormous, and his ministers wanted him removed.

A group of doctors declared him unfit to rule, without examining him in person. On 12 June 1886, he was taken from Neuschwanstein. The next day, he and one of those doctors were found dead in the shallow water of Lake Starnberg. How they died is still a mystery. Only about 15 of the more than 200 planned rooms were ever finished. Some halls are still bare brick today, and visitors never see them.

Seven weeks after Ludwig's death, the castle opened to visitors. The king had wanted it to be private, but tickets helped pay off his debts.

Today it is one of the most visited castles in Europe, with about 1.4 million visitors a year before 2020. Most walk up a steep road or ride in a horse-drawn carriage. A nearby footbridge called Marienbrücke, over a deep gorge, gives the view seen on postcards.

In 2025, UNESCO named Neuschwanstein a World Heritage Site, together with Ludwig's other palaces, Linderhof, Herrenchiemsee and the King's House on Schachen.

Walt Disney and his wife visited Europe in the 1930s and saw castles in Germany. When his designers created Sleeping Beauty Castle for Disneyland in 1955, they took ideas from Neuschwanstein and other European castles. Later Disney castles, including Cinderella Castle in Florida, borrowed from Neuschwanstein too, along with French palaces.

Real [[@knights-castles|medieval castles]] were usually squat and grey, built to survive sieges. Thanks partly to Ludwig, many children around the world now picture something tall, white and pointed when they hear the word "castle". That is why [[@disney-parks|theme parks]], storybooks and cartoons all seem to share the same castle.

text: There is no single American food, in the same way there is no single Indian food. The United States is a huge country of immigrants. Its food is a mix of what Native Americans grew, what Europeans brought, what enslaved Africans cooked, and what newer arrivals from Mexico, China, Italy, India and elsewhere added.

Some of it is famous everywhere: [[@burgers-hotdogs|burgers and hot dogs]], fried chicken, [[@pancakes-world|pancakes]], apple pie and pizza. But a fisherman in Maine, a rancher in Texas and a grandmother in Louisiana would each give you a very different answer if you asked what "American food" means at home.

st.reveal: Turkeys are native to North America, and people in Mexico tamed them long ago. Apple pie came from England, and hot dogs came with German immigrants in the 1800s.

myth: Apple pie was invented in America.

English cookbooks had apple pie recipes by the late 1300s, long before Europeans settled in America. Apples themselves came to North America with European settlers. The saying "as American as apple pie" is much newer than the pie.

sec.t:
Long before Europeans arrived, the [[@native-nations|Native nations]] of North America were skilled farmers. Many grew the "[[@corn-maize|Three Sisters]]" together in one field. Maize grew tall, beans climbed up the maize stalks, and broad squash leaves shaded the soil and kept weeds down.

The Americas also gave the world turkey, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, [[@peanut-butter|peanuts]], [[@food-vanilla|vanilla]] and chocolate, though many of these were first grown farther south, in Mexico and South America. Wild rice, cranberries and maple syrup come from the north. When Indians eat aloo or tamatar today, they are eating foods that first crossed an ocean from the Americas.

American food changes from region to region. New England, in the north-east, is known for clam chowder, a creamy seafood soup, and lobster rolls. The South has fried chicken, cornbread, biscuits and [[@bbq|slow-smoked barbecue]].

In Louisiana, French, Spanish, African and Native cooking blended into Creole and Cajun food. Gumbo is a thick stew of seafood or sausage, thickened with okra, served over rice. [[@new-orleans|New Orleans]] is famous for it. In the south-west, food mixes with Mexican cooking, and in California, fresh vegetables and Asian flavours are everywhere.

In 1940, two brothers named Richard and Maurice McDonald opened a drive-in restaurant in San Bernardino, California. A few years later they redesigned it to make burgers quickly on an assembly line, like a factory. Many other chains copied the idea, and [[@fast-food-history|American fast food]] spread around the world.

In India, these chains had to change their menus. Many outlets sell no beef, and offer paneer, aloo tikki and spicy chicken burgers instead. It is a good example of how food bends to fit wherever it goes.

sec.h: The biggest meal of the year
sec.t: On the fourth Thursday of November, many American families eat a [[@thanksgiving|Thanksgiving]] dinner. Roast turkey sits beside stuffing, mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and pumpkin pie. Almost every one of those foods has roots in the Americas. Families from Indian, Mexican or Chinese backgrounds often add their own dishes, which may be the most American touch of all.

text: Punjabi food is hearty farm food from the plains of northwest [[@pakistan-history|India and Pakistan]]. Punjab means "land of five rivers", and its [[fertile|fertile]] fields grow wheat, [[@mustard|mustard]], maize and sugarcane. Meals centre on wheat rotis, rich dals, seasonal greens, and plenty of milk, curd, butter and ghee.

The tandoor, a big clay oven, gives Punjabi cooking its smoky breads and grilled meats. After 1947, Punjabi [[refugee|refugees]] carried this food to Delhi and beyond, opening roadside dhabas and restaurants. Dishes like butter chicken and dal makhani became famous worldwide, though they're more restaurant food than everyday home cooking.

sec.t:
Punjab's land is flat and well watered by rivers and canals. In the 1960s and 1970s, the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]] brought new seeds, [[fertiliser|fertilisers]] and [[irrigation|irrigation]], and Punjab became one of India's biggest producers of wheat and rice.

{{story:green-revolution}}

Wheat is the everyday grain. Rotis are cooked on a flat iron tawa, and parathas, stuffed with potato, cauliflower or radish, are eaten with white butter for breakfast.

In winter, when mustard plants grow tall and green, families cook sarson ka saag. The leaves are slow-cooked and mashed, then eaten with makki ki roti, a flatbread made from maize flour, topped with butter and [[@jaggery|jaggery]] on the side.

A tandoor is a large clay pot, often sunk into the ground or set in a brick frame, with a fire at the bottom. It gets extremely hot. Bakers slap dough onto its inner wall, where it puffs and chars in a minute or two.

Village communities once shared a common tandoor, where women would bring dough to be baked. Today, tandoori rotis, naans and kulchas are mostly made in dhabas and restaurants. Amritsar is famous for its stuffed kulchas, crisp outside and soft inside.

Punjabi families traditionally kept buffaloes and cows, and dairy shows up at almost every meal. Curd is served with food, and lassi, curd whisked with water and sugar or salt, is served in tall steel glasses.

Ghee and white butter, churned at home, add richness to dal and rotis. Hard farm work in the fields once burned off all those [[calorie|calories]].

At gurdwaras, Sikh places of worship, there is a free community kitchen called the langar. The custom was started by the first Sikh Guru, Guru Nanak, in the 1500s and spread by later [[@sikh-gurus|Gurus]]. Anyone may eat, whatever their religion or background, sitting side by side on the floor.

The langar at the [[@golden-temple|Golden Temple]] in [[@amritsar|Amritsar]] is one of the biggest free kitchens in the world. Volunteers chop vegetables, roll rotis and wash dishes for tens of thousands of visitors a day, and on busy days around one lakh. The food is simple: dal, roti, a vegetable and kheer.

In 1947, the [[@partition|Partition]] of India split Punjab between India and Pakistan. Millions of people were forced to move. Many Punjabi refugees settled in Delhi and opened small eateries.

One such eatery, Moti Mahal, became famous for tandoori chicken. Butter chicken, pieces of tandoori chicken in a buttery tomato gravy, came from Delhi restaurants in the years after Partition. Two restaurant families have argued in court over who deserves the credit.

From Delhi, Punjabi restaurant food spread across India and to cities like London, Toronto and New York. Many people abroad think of it as simply "Indian food".

text: It depends on where you live. In many cities in the United States, Europe and parts of India, tap water is treated, tested many times a day and safe to drink. There, bottled water is not healthier. It just costs far more and creates plastic waste.

In places where tap water is not safe, because pipes leak, rivers are polluted or treatment is patchy, sealed bottled water can protect people from illness. That is why many Indian families boil water, use [[@water-tech|filters at home]] or buy large cans of purified water. So the honest answer is that it depends on the tap.

Bottled water is not automatically cleaner. In places with good water treatment, tap water is tested often and meets strict rules. Where tap water is unsafe, though, sealed bottled water or purified water at home is a sensible choice.

sec.t:
In the United States, the Safe Drinking Water Act of 1974 lets the government set limits for germs, metals and chemicals in public water. Water companies must test regularly and report the results.

Bottled water is treated as a packaged food and checked by a different agency. Its rules are similar, but tap water is often tested more often. Several big bottled brands even start with city water and filter it again. A litre of bottled water can cost hundreds of times more than a litre from the tap.

Tap water is only as good as the pipes and plants behind it. In 2014 the city of Flint, Michigan, switched its water source to save money. The new water ate into old pipes and released lead, a metal that harms children's brains. For years many families had to drink bottled water.

In India, many towns do not have water that is safe straight from the tap. In 2019 the Government of India started the Jal Jeevan Mission, which aims to bring piped water to every rural home. Making that water safe to drink is the next big task.

Many Indian homes treat their own water. [[@boiling-water|Boiling]] kills germs. Candle filters strain out dirt. UV purifiers kill [[microbe|microbes]] with light. Reverse osmosis machines, known as RO, push water through a very fine membrane that blocks salts and many chemicals.

RO systems have a cost: they usually waste a good share of the water that goes in, and can remove useful minerals too. Bottled water sold in India must meet standards set by the Bureau of Indian Standards and carry its mark.

Every drop, from a tap or a bottle, has travelled through the [[@water-cycle|water cycle]]. It has fallen as rain, run through rivers or soaked underground, and evaporated again, over and over for billions of years.

Some bottling plants pump large amounts of groundwater from one place, which can upset local people who depend on the same wells. In parts of India and the United States, communities have protested against plants taking water during [[@droughts|droughts]].

A good rule is to find out about your local water. Many cities publish test reports. If your tap water is safe, a refillable steel bottle is cheaper and creates almost no waste. If it is not, bottled water or a reliable home purifier keeps you healthy. Either way, drinking enough water matters far more than which bottle it comes from.
